jQMC: A JAX-based ab initio quantum Monte Carlo package designed for GPU-accelerated computing

Kousuke Nakano Email: kousuke_1123@icloud.com Affiliation: Center for Basic Research on Materials, National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS), 1-2-1 Sengen, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-0047, Japan    Michele Casula Affiliation: Institut de Minéralogie, de Physique des Matériaux et de Cosmochimie (IMPMC), Sorbonne Université, CNRS UMR 7590, IRD UMR 206, MNHN, 4 Place Jussieu, 75252 Paris, France
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We present jQMC, a Python-based computational package for ab initio Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, designed for modern GPU-accelerated computing environments. jQMC implements two well-established QMC algorithms: Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) and the lattice-regularized variant of Diffusion Monte Carlo (LRDMC). The employed wave function is a Jastrow factor combined with the antisymmetrized geminal power with spin-singlet and spin-triplet pairings, which contains the single Slater determinant as its special lowest-rank case. The wave function can be initialized from external Hartree-Fock/Density Functional Theory calculations through the TREX-IO library (a common wave-function format across electronic-structure packages) and optimized by stochastic reconfiguration and linear-method energy minimization. One of the prominent features of jQMC is its use of JAX, which enables automatic differentiation for wave function optimization and atomic force calculations, and allows the main QMC algorithms to be Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled and portable across CPU and GPU. jQMC is vectorized over walkers at the top level of the QMC algorithms, providing efficient intra-GPU (CPU) vectorization. The multi-GPU (CPU) parallelization is also supported through MPI and JAX sharding. To assess the practical performance of this implementation, we benchmarked jQMC performance on NVIDIA GPUs (A100 and H100) and analyzed CUDA kernels. For the test cases analyzed here, with system sizes up to 160 electrons, the current version of jQMC is faster than TurboRVB, a Fortran90 code implementing the same algorithms and wave functions, once jQMC is run on GPUs. In terms of wall-time, the gain can reach an order of magnitude for VMC, while it is more moderate for LRDMC. Furthermore, to demonstrate the applications of jQMC, we focus on an ongoing debate in the community, namely the accuracy of QMC quantities compared with highly accurate Quantum Chemistry calculations such as coupled-cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]. We studied the accuracy of atomic forces computed by VMC and LRDMC for ethanol and malonaldehyde. We found that LRDMC forces achieve ∼\sim 1.5 kcal/mol/Å accuracy in the mean absolute error (MAE) with respect to all-electron CCSD(T) forces for ethanol, while LRDMC and CCSD(T) forces are quite different (∼\sim 5 kcal/mol/Å in MAE) for malonaldehyde.

I Introduction

Solving the many-body Schrödinger equation remains a central challenge in computational chemistry and physics. For nearly a century, researchers have been developing many theoretical and numerical techniques to address this problem. Among these, Density Functional Theory (DFT) is one of the most widely adopted approaches. DFT maps the many-electron problem into a system of non-interacting electrons in an effective potential, called eXchange-Correlation (XC) functional [35]. Although DFT is formally exact, its practical application depends on the XC functional, and its exact form remains unknown. Progress in systematically improving this functional has been elusive [38]. As a result, widely used approximations often fail in situations involving strong correlation effects or weak van der Waals interactions.

An alternative strategy for addressing the complexity of the many-electron Schrödinger equation is offered by ab initio Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods [25, 8]. Unlike conventional deterministic approaches, QMC leverages stochastic sampling (i.e., Monte Carlo) to evaluate expectation values, thereby bypassing some of the limitations of deterministic methods. The theoretical foundation of QMC dates back to the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) in the 1940s [40] and fixed-node Diffusion Monte Carlo (FN-DMC) in the 1980s [17, 18], which have since become indispensable across diverse scientific communities. QMC shows a favorable scaling with system size, albeit with a larger prefactor than in mean-field approaches. This prefactor, however, is mitigated by the nature of MCMC, which makes QMC suited for modern high-performance computing (HPC) architectures. The algorithmic structure allows for near-perfect weak scaling across thousands of cores, positioning QMC as a promising method for next-generation simulations of both molecular and extended systems.

To dates, several groups have implemented ab initio QMC codes such as Amolqc, CASINO [53, 54], CHAMP-EU[73], CHAMP-US[5], CMQMC, PyQMC [95], QMC=Chem[71], QMCPACK [32, 31], QMeCha[7], QWalk[93], and TurboRVB [45, 47] (named alphabetically). It is also worth highlighting recent efforts for standardizing data and functionalities required among QMC packages. For instance, TREX-IO [62] is a library designed to standardize the wave function format among different QMC packages. QMCkl [75] provides common kernels for core QMC algorithms. They represent valuable efforts in the QMC community to consolidate their development efforts.

The recent shift of HPC facilities toward GPU-dominated infrastructures presents significant challenges for scientific computing and programming [74]. Legacy codebases cannot fully exploit the computational power of GPU hardware without a comprehensive refactoring of the code because the suitable designs are often very different between them. Nearly all of the top-tier systems, such as those ranked in the TOP500 list [84, 87], are equipped with CPU-GPU hybrid architectures, with very few exceptions such as Fugaku [70]. There are several approaches to make codebases portable to GPU machines, such as using native programming languages (e.g., CUDA), directive-based programming models (e.g., OpenACC [96]), or OpenMP offload, and exploiting GPU-optimized libraries such as NVIDIA’s cuBLAS and cuSOLVER. A related and increasingly promising approach involves harnessing libraries, such as Kokkos [23, 89], TensorFlow [1], PyTorch [57], and JAX [11], which are designed inherently with GPU execution. These frameworks offer a powerful abstraction for high-performance computing and are now being explored for ab initio QMC applications. Notable examples of ab initio QMC codes built on these modern frameworks include FermiNet [61], PauliNet [29], QMCTorch [66], and JaQMC [65] which have demonstrated the potential of combining QMC with machine learning and neural network architectures.

Our developing ab initio QMC code, named jQMC, relies on one of the libraries, JAX [11]. JAX has several features helping with making code fast and portable across different architectures. jQMC implements two ground-state QMC algorithms: variational Monte Carlo (VMC) and DMC [25] in its lattice regularized version. In VMC, the ground state is obtained by minimizing the total energy (or variance) with a parametrized many-body wave function ansatz. DMC is an imaginary-time projection technique [8] that filters out the ground-state wave function from a given trial wave function, typically combined with the so-called fixed-node (FN) approximation. The nodal surface is constructed by a mean-field calculation, such as Hartree-Fock (HF) or DFT, or by an accurate variational optimization, and is usually kept frozen during the projection.

In particular, the jQMC package introduces several distinguishing features that collectively enhance its capability and flexibility for ab initio quantum Monte Carlo simulations: (i)\rm(\hskip 1.79993pti\hskip 1.79993pt) wave function ansatz: jQMC supports the Jastrow Antisymmetrized Geminal Power (JAGP) [14], a resonating valence bond (RVB)-type wave function. JAGP contains the single Slater determinant as a special case. (ii)\rm(\hskip 1.79993ptii\hskip 1.79993pt) wave function optimization: The code implements the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) method [81] and the linear method (LM), robust and efficient optimization algorithms that enable simultaneous optimization of both wave function amplitudes and nodal surfaces. (iii)\rm(\hskip 1.79993ptiii\hskip 1.79993pt) Projection method: To perform DMC calculations with enhanced numerical control, jQMC includes an implementation of the lattice regularized DMC (LRDMC) method [13], which provides improved stability over traditional DMC algorithms. (iv)\rm(\hskip 1.79993ptiv\hskip 1.79993pt) Force evaluation: By leveraging algorithmic differentiation with the JAX framework, jQMC enables efficient implementation of energy derivatives, such as atomic forces [79], directly from the many-body wave function. (v)\rm(\hskip 1.79993ptv\hskip 1.79993pt) Software architecture: Developed in Python, the codebase emphasizes ease of use for end-users and modular extensibility for developers. This makes it well-suited for both production simulations and the rapid prototyping of new QMC algorithms. (vi)\rm(\hskip 1.79993ptvi\hskip 1.79993pt) Hardware acceleration: Through just-in-time (JIT) compilation and vectorized execution (e.g., via jit and vmap) provided by JAX, jQMC achieves high computational performance across diverse hardware backends, including CPUs and GPUs. (vii)\rm(\hskip 1.79993ptvii\hskip 1.79993pt) Parallel scalability: Built-in MPI support (mpi4py [69]) and the native JAX sharding mechanism allow jQMC to scale efficiently on modern HPC platforms, enabling large-scale many-body simulations. These components together position jQMC as a modern and versatile platform for both conducting accurate quantum Monte Carlo simulations and developing novel methodologies within the QMC framework.

This paper is organized as follows: Sec. II briefly explains the QMC algorithms implemented in jQMC, MCMC, VMC, and LRDMC. Sec. III describes the RVB-family of wave functions combined with the Jastrow factor; Sec. IV focuses on the implementation of the bare Coulomb interactions and effective core potentials. Sec. V details how energy derivatives are computed (e.g., atomic forces) in jQMC; Sec. VI reviews the wave function optimization techniques currently implemented in jQMC; Sec. VII summarizes the implementation of jQMC and its typical QMC workflow; Sec. VIII describes the mixed-precision support implemented in jQMC. Sec. IX explains the vectorization strategy employed in jQMC and its benchmark results measured on Miyabi (University of Tokyo) supercomputer; Sec. X reports an analysis of the CUDA kernels in jQMC using NVIDIA Nsight Systems and NVIDIA Nsight Compute, and study the bottlenecks of the current implementation. Sec. XI reports wall-time benchmarks of jQMC on CPU and GPU machines, and compares them with the TurboRVB QMC code, implementing the same algorithms and wave functions; Sec. XII describes the parallelization strategy employed in jQMC and reports weak scaling results of jQMC, measured on Leonardo (CINECA) and Miyabi (University of Tokyo) supercomputers; Sec. XIII reports a validation of jQMC by comparing the total energies of methane, water, and methane-water dimer, and its binding energy with other QMC codes; Sec. XIV demonstrates MCMC and DMC atomic-force calculations for the ethanol and malonaldehyde molecules, and compares them with all-electron coupled-cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)].

II Methods

jQMC implements two established Quantum Monte Carlo methods: Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) and Lattice Regularized Diffusion Monte Carlo (LRDMC). We summarize these methods in this Section. For further details, the reader is referred to more comprehensive reviews and textbooks on QMC [25, 8]. We notice that throughout this paper the formalism is presented assuming a real many-body wave function Ψ⁡(𝐱)∈ℝ\Psi(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}, which is also the only case currently supported by the jQMC implementation (v.0.2.2). Extending the formalism to a complex wave function Ψ⁡(𝐱)∈ℂ\Psi(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{C} is left for future developments.

II.1 Variational Monte Carlo

Given the ab initio Hamiltonian ℋ^\hat{\mathcal{H}}, the expectation value of the energy can be computed by MCMC as:

for a given wave function (WF) Ψ\Psi, where 𝐱=(𝐫1​σ1,𝐫2​σ2,…​𝐫N​σN){\mathbf{x}}=\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}}{\sigma_{1}},{{\mathbf{r}}_{2}}{\sigma_{2}},\ldots{{\mathbf{r}}_{N}}{\sigma_{N}}}\right) represents the NN electron coordinates and their spins, and

eL​(𝐱)≡ℋ^​Ψ​(𝐱)Ψ⁡(𝐱)andπ⁡(𝐱)≡Ψ2​(𝐱)∫d​𝐱′​Ψ2​(𝐱′),{e_{L}}\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)\equiv{\hat{\mathcal{H}}\Psi\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)\over\Psi\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)}\quad\text{and}\quad\pi\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)\equiv{{\Psi^{2}}\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)\over\int{d{\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}{\Psi^{2}}\left({\mathbf{x^{\prime}}}\right)}},

are the local energy and the probability distribution, respectively. MCMC allows one to evaluate the multidimensional integration in Eq. 1 stochastically by generating a set of configurations {𝐱i}\left\{{{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right\} according to the distribution π⁡(𝐱)\pi\left({\mathbf{x}}\right) and by averaging the accumulated local energies eL​(𝐱i){e_{L}}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right):

EMCMC=⟨eL​(𝐱)⟩π⁡(𝐱)≈1M​∑i=1MeL​(𝐱i),{E_{{\text{MCMC}}}}={\left\langle{{e_{L}}\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)}\right\rangle_{\pi\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)}}\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{M}{{e_{L}}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right)}, (2)

EMCMC​(α)=∫d​𝐱​eL​(𝐱,α)​π​(𝐱,α)⩾E0,{E_{{\text{MCMC}}}}\left(\alpha\right)=\int{d{\mathbf{x}}{e_{L}}\left({{\mathbf{x}},\alpha}\right)\pi\left({{\mathbf{x}},\alpha}\right)}\geqslant E_{0}, (3)

where, according to the variational theorem, EMCMC{E_{\text{MCMC}}} provides an upper bound to the exact ground-state energy (E0E_{0}). This framework is called VMC.

One of the key implementations of VMC is the MCMC evaluation of the Hamiltonian expectation value and the update of the parameters of the trial WF anstaz ΨT\Psi_{T}, to get the best variational representation of the ground state according to the variational principle. The possible WF parametrizations available in jQMC are discussed later. The MCMC implemented in jQMC relies on the generalized Metropolis algorithm (Metropolis–Hastings algorithm [39, 27]). The acceptance of a proposed move (𝒜⁡(𝐱→𝐱′CLOSE\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}^{\prime})) reads:

𝒜⁡(𝐱→𝐱′)=min⁡[1,Ψ2​(𝐱′)Ψ2​(𝐱)⋅T⁡(𝐱′→𝐱)T⁡(𝐱→𝐱′)],\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\min\left[1,\frac{\Psi^{2}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})}{\Psi^{2}(\mathbf{x})}\cdot\frac{T(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathbf{x})}{T(\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}^{\prime})}\right], (4)

where 𝐱={⋯,𝐫l,⋯}\mathbf{x}=\{\cdots,\mathbf{r}_{l},\cdots\} and 𝐱′={⋯,𝐫l′,⋯}\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\{\cdots,\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{l},\cdots\} differ by a single-electron position. σprop​(𝐫l)=1ZI⁡(l)2​|𝐫l−𝐑I⁡(l)|⋅1+ZI⁡(l)2​|𝐫l−𝐑I⁡(l)|1+|𝐫l−𝐑I⁡(l)|,\sigma_{\rm prop}(\mathbf{r}_{l})=\frac{1}{Z_{I(l)}^{2}|\mathbf{r}_{l}-\mathbf{R}_{I(l)}|}\cdot\frac{1+Z_{I(l)}^{2}|\mathbf{r}_{l}-\mathbf{R}_{I(l)}|}{1+|\mathbf{r}_{l}-\mathbf{R}_{I(l)}|}, (5)

to satisfy the detailed-balance condition. Thus, its ratio becomes:

T⁡(𝐱′→𝐱)T⁡(𝐱→𝐱′)=(σprop​(𝐫l)σprop​(𝐫l′))​exp⁡[−|𝐫l−𝐫l′|2​(12​(σprop​(𝐫l′)​Δ​t)2−12​(σprop​(𝐫l)​Δ​t)2)].\cfrac{T(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathbf{x})}{T(\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}^{\prime})}=\left(\cfrac{\sigma_{\rm prop}(\mathbf{r}_{l})}{\sigma_{\rm prop}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{l})}\right)\exp\left[{-|\mathbf{r}_{l}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{l}|^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2(\sigma_{\rm prop}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{l})\Delta t)^{2}}-\frac{1}{2(\sigma_{\rm prop}(\mathbf{r}_{l})\Delta t)^{2}}\right)}\right]. Following this transition probability, we repeatedly perform accept/reject steps to generate Monte Carlo samples and evaluate Eq. 2. Eqs. 5 and 7 automatically modulate the amplitude of the MCMC step, by reaching a higher sampling efficiency according to the distribution of the electronic clouds centered around each nucleus.

II.2 Lattice regularized Monte Carlo

II.2.1 Formalism of Lattice regularized diffusion Monte Carlo (LRDMC)

Lattice regularized diffusion Monte Carlo (LRDMC) [13] is a method built to filter out the ground state WF |Υ0⟩{\left|{{\Upsilon_{0}}}\right\rangle} from a given guidance WF |ΨT⟩\left|{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}}\right\rangle. This method is based on Green’s function Monte Carlo (GFMC) [86, 12, 78], and thus, it is sometimes called “power method”. In the GFMC formalism, the ground-state WF can be obtained by iteratively applying (λ−ℋ^)M{\left({\lambda-\hat{\mathcal{H}}}\right)^{M}} to a given trial wave function:

|Υ0⟩∝limM→∞(λ−ℋ^)M|ΨT⟩=limM→∞(λ−E0)M[a0|Υ0⟩+∑n≠0(λ−Enλ−E0)Man|Υn⟩],\begin{split}\left|{{\Upsilon_{0}}}\right\rangle&\propto\mathop{\lim}\limits_{M\to\infty}{\left({\lambda-\hat{\mathcal{H}}}\right)^{M}}\left|{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}}\right\rangle\\ &=\mathop{\lim}\limits_{M\to\infty}{\left({\lambda-{E_{0}}}\right)^{M}}\left[{{a_{0}}\left|{{\Upsilon_{0}}}\right\rangle+\sum\limits_{n\neq 0}{{{\left({\frac{{\lambda-{E_{n}}}}{{\lambda-{E_{0}}}}}\right)}^{M}}{a_{n}}\left|{{\Upsilon_{n}}}\right\rangle}}\right],\end{split} (16)

where λ\lambda is a large positive number, En{{E_{n}}} is nn-th eigenvalue of ℋ^\hat{\mathcal{H}}, and an{a_{n}} is the coefficient for the nn-th eigenvectors (Υn{{\Upsilon_{n}}}) (i.e. |ΨT⟩=∑nan|Υn⟩\left|{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}}\right\rangle=\sum\limits_{n}{{a_{n}}\left|{{\Upsilon_{n}}}\right\rangle}). The above projection filters out the ground state WF Υ0{{\Upsilon_{0}}} from a given guidance WF |ΨT⟩\left|{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}}\right\rangle unless the trial WF is orthogonal to the ground state (i.e., a0≡⟨ΨT|Υ0⟩≠0{a_{0}}\equiv\braket{{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}}|{{\Upsilon_{0}}}}\neq 0) and |λ−En|/|λ−E0|≥1|{\lambda-{E_{n}}}|/|{\lambda-{E_{0}}}|\geq 1.

For fermions (electrons), LRDMC is always associated with the fixed-node (FN) approximation [8] because the Green’s function it not always positive for fermions. This is referred to as the sign problem. Therefore, in LRDMC, the Hamiltonian is modified by setting to zero the “wrong” sign terms and summing them up into the spin-flip term 𝒱sf(𝐱)=∑𝐱′:s𝐱′,𝐱>0ℋ𝐱′,𝐱ΨT(𝐱′)/ΨT(𝐱){\mathcal{V}_{{\rm{sf}}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)=\sum\limits_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}:{s_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}>0}{{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}/{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right). This defines an effective FN Hamiltonian ℋ^FN\hat{\mathcal{H}}^{\text{FN}}, which reads as:

ℋ𝐱′,𝐱FN={ℋ𝐱,𝐱+𝒱SF​(𝐱)​for​𝐱′=𝐱,ℋ𝐱′,𝐱for​𝐱′≠𝐱,s𝐱′,𝐱<0,0for​𝐱′≠𝐱,s𝐱′,𝐱>0,{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}^{\text{FN}}=\begin{cases}{{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}}}+{\mathcal{V}_{{\rm{SF}}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)\,\,\,\,{\rm{for}}\,\,\,\,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}=\mathbf{x},\\ {{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{\rm{for}}\,\,\,\,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\neq\mathbf{x},{s_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}<0,\\ 0\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{\rm{for}}\,\,\,\,\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\neq\mathbf{x},{s_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}>0,\end{cases} (17)

where s𝐱′,𝐱=ΨT​(𝐱)​ℋ𝐱′,𝐱​ΨT​(𝐱′){s_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}={\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right){{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right) (i.e, s𝐱′,𝐱>0{s_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}}>0 indicates that the 𝐱→𝐱′\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}^{\prime} crosses the nodal surface of the guiding function, or simply contributes to the Green’s function λ−ℋ^\lambda-\hat{\mathcal{H}} with the “wrong” sign). The fixed-node Green’s function with the guiding function is then:

𝒢𝐱′,𝐱FN=(λ​δ𝐱′,𝐱−ℋ𝐱′,𝐱FN)​ΨT​(𝐱′)ΨT​(𝐱)=λ​δ𝐱′,𝐱−ΨT​(𝐱′)ΨT​(𝐱)​ℋ𝐱′,𝐱FN{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}^{{\text{FN}}}=\left({\lambda\delta_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}-{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}^{{\text{FN}}}}\right)\frac{{\Psi_{\text{T}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}}{{\Psi_{\text{T}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)}}={\lambda}\delta_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}-\frac{{\Psi_{\text{T}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}}{{\Psi_{\text{T}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)}}{\mathcal{H}}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}^{{\text{FN}}} (18)

prevents walkers from crossing the nodal surface.

In LRDMC, the original continuous Hamiltonian is discretized with electron hopping with step size aa. The corresponding Hamiltonian ℋ^a{{\hat{\mathcal{H}}}^{a}} satisfies ℋ^a→ℋ^{{{\hat{\mathcal{H}}}^{a}}}\to{\hat{\mathcal{H}}} for a→0a\to 0. In other words, the kinetic and potential parts are approximated by a discretized form, ℋ^a≡K^a+V^a{{{\hat{\mathcal{H}}}^{a}}}\equiv\hat{K}^{a}+\hat{V}^{a}. The discretized kinetic term is computed via the finite-difference Laplacian ∇a2\nabla_{a}^{2} acting on a function f⁡(xi,yi,zi)f\left({{x_{i}},{y_{i}},{z_{i}}}\right) as

∇a,i2​f​(xi,yi,zi)=1a2​{[f⁡(xi+a)−f⁡(xi)]+[f⁡(xi−a)−f⁡(xi)]}↔yi↔zi.\nabla^{2}_{a,i}f\left({{x_{i}},{y_{i}},{z_{i}}}\right)=\frac{1}{{{a^{2}}}}\left\{{\left[{f\left({{x_{i}}+a}\right)-f\left({{x_{i}}}\right)}\right]+\left[{f\left({{x_{i}}-a}\right)-f\left({{x_{i}}}\right)}\right]}\right\}\leftrightarrow{y_{i}}\leftrightarrow{z_{i}}. (19)

More specifically, the discretized kinetic operator K^a≡−12∑i∇2i,a\hat{K}^{a}\equiv-\cfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\nabla^{2}_{i,a} acts on |x⟩\ket{x} as:

K^a|x⟩≡−12∑i=1Ne∇2a,i|x⟩=3​Nea2|x⟩−12​a2∑j=16​Ne|xj⟩,\displaystyle\hat{K}^{a}\ket{x}\equiv-\cfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{e}}\nabla^{2}_{a,i}\ket{x}=\cfrac{3N_{e}}{a^{2}}\ket{x}-\cfrac{1}{2a^{2}}\sum_{j=1}^{6N_{e}}\ket{x_{j}}, (20)

leading to

K^𝐱′,𝐱a​ΨT​(𝐱′)ΨT​(𝐱)=3​Nea2​δ𝐱′,𝐱−12​a2​ΨT​(𝐱′)ΨT​(𝐱)​δ𝐱′,𝐱a​d,\displaystyle\hat{K}^{a}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}\frac{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)}=\cfrac{3N_{e}}{a^{2}}\delta_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}-\cfrac{1}{2a^{2}}\frac{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)}\delta^{ad}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}, (21)

where δ𝐱′,𝐱a​d=1\delta^{ad}_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime},\mathbf{x}}=1 only if 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} is adjacent to 𝐱\mathbf{x}, otherwise 0. Here, the point is that one should consider only 6​Ne6N_{e} 𝐱′\mathbf{x}^{\prime} adjacent to 𝐱\mathbf{x}, making the GFMC approach applicable to the continuum ab initio Hamiltonian. The 6NeN_{e} wave function ratios (ΨT​(𝐱′)/ΨT​(𝐱)\Psi_{\text{T}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)/{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)) are computed in practice using the fast update method, described in Subsec. III.5, which is critically important for a fast calculation of LRDMC. Once the kinetic term is discretized, the potential term V^a\hat{V}^{a} is defined in such a way that the local energy of ℋ^a\hat{\mathcal{H}}^{a} computed on the trial WF coincides with the local energy of the continuous Hamiltonian ℋ^\hat{\mathcal{H}}. In practice V^a\hat{V}^{a} is divided into local and non-local terms, V^a≡V^loca+V^nl{\hat{V}^{a}}\equiv\hat{V}_{\rm loc}^{a}+\hat{V}_{\rm nl}, where only the local term depends on the discretized mesh aa. The non-local potential operator V^nl\hat{V}_{\rm nl} exists only in the calculations with effective core potentials (ECPs). The details of the non-local potential operator are described in Sec. IV.

II.2.2 Implementation of LRDMC algorithms

Since several papers have already described the details of the LRDMC implementation [15, 13, 8, 45, 48, 52], we do not repeat them here. jQMC implements two LRDMC algorithms: the original (conventional) LRDMC scheme [13] and the recently developed load-balanced scheme [52]. In the conventional algorithm, for a given projection time τ\tau, the electrons are moved a number of times corresponding to the application of the projector exp⁡(−τ​H^)\exp(-\tau\hat{H}), and branching (reconfiguration) is then performed. Because this number is determined stochastically, the number of electron moves varies from walker to walker. As a result, in large-scale parallel calculations, load imbalance develops among walkers, which degrades weak scaling [52]. To remove this problem, we recently proposed an alternative algorithm in which all walkers perform the same number of projection steps, and demonstrated that this substantially improves weak scaling [52]. Both algorithms are implemented in jQMC.

Here, we focus on one implementation aspect that has received less attention in the literature, namely the branching (reconfiguration) step [8], especially its MPI implementation involving inter-node communication. In LRDMC, regardless of whether the conventional or load-balanced algorithm is used, branching (reconfiguration) [8] is carried out as follows. Every NprojN_{\rm proj} projections, the code performs a branching step:

  1. (1)

    New walkers are selected from the previous population with probability proportional to their weights before branching:

    pα,n=wα,n∑βwβ,n.p_{\alpha,n}=\frac{w_{\alpha,n}}{\sum_{\beta}w_{\beta,n}}. (22)
  2. (2)

    The weights of all new walkers are reset to the average weight of the previous population:

    wα,n+1=w¯n≡1Nw​∑βwβ,n∀α.w_{\alpha,n+1}=\bar{w}_{n}\equiv\frac{1}{N_{w}}\sum_{\beta}w_{\beta,n}\qquad\forall\alpha. (23)

In the multi-walker formalism, the walker state therefore carries an additional walker index α\alpha, namely (xα,n,wα,n)(x_{\alpha,n},w_{\alpha,n}). The selection of new configurations is implemented using an efficient reconfiguration scheme in which the surviving walkers are chosen from NwN_{w} correlated random numbers [8]:

Zα=ξ+α−1Nw,α=1,…,Nw,Z_{\alpha}=\frac{\xi+\alpha-1}{N_{w}},\qquad\alpha=1,\ldots,N_{w}, (24)

where ξ\xi is a uniform random number in [0,1)[0,1). These numbers are compared with the cumulative normalized weights to determine the new walker population. In our calculations, the survival rate is typically around 90%, and most walkers survive unchanged after each branching step. Therefore, when walker replication and deletion are communicated across MPI ranks, all-to-all communication is unnecessary. Instead, point-to-point communication is sufficient, and this is essential for achieving good weak scaling. It is also important to perform communications simultaneously with the other computations associated with reconfiguration, that is, to use asynchronous communication so that data transfer does not become a bottleneck.

II.3 Error analysis

To estimate the mean and variance of an observable O^\hat{O} from a Monte Carlo simulation, one accumulates its local values along the MCMC samples. Statistical efficiency is gained by running multiple independent MCMC chains in parallel. Let i∈{1,…,M}i\in\{1,\ldots,M\}, where MM is the chain length, be the MCMC step index in a chain, and n∈{1,…,N}n\in\{1,\ldots,N\} the index for an independent chain; Xi,nX_{i,n} is the electron configuration at the ii-th step of the nn-th chain, and Oi,n≡O^​(Xi,n)O_{i,n}\equiv\hat{O}(X_{i,n}) are the accumulated local values. The autocorrelation of MCMC samples within a chain causes the naive independent and identically distributed (iid) variance estimator to underestimate the true variance of the sample mean, leading to underestimation of error bars. To mitigate this problem, one usually uses two techniques, reblocking and jackknife resampling [8].

Let bb be the block (bin) size and Mb=⌊M/b⌋M_{b}=\lfloor M/b\rfloor the resulting number of binned samples per chain. One defines the binned samples Oj,nO_{j,n} with j∈{1,…,Mb}j\in\{1,\ldots,M_{b}\} as Oj,n=(1/b)​∑i∈ℬjOi,nO_{j,n}=(1/b)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{j}}O_{i,n}, where ℬj={(j−1)​b+1,…,j​b}\mathcal{B}_{j}=\{(j-1)b+1,\dots,jb\} is the index set of MCMC steps belonging to the jj-th block. When the block size bb exceeds the autocorrelation time, the binned samples become effectively independent, so naive iid-based variance estimators recover the correct standard error of the mean. We notice that samples from different chains are already mutually independent, so blocking is performed only along the in-chain direction ii and never across the chain direction nn.

When the statistical estimator is a nonlinear function of the Monte Carlo samples, such as a ratio estimator like the DMC/LRDMC mixed average, resampling techniques are required to estimate its uncertainty accurately. jQMC employs the so-called jackknife method to estimate the mean and variance of the accumulated observables. First, one flattens the binned samples {Oj,n}\{O_{j,n}\} into a single sequence {Ol}l=1NJ\{O_{l}\}_{l=1}^{N_{J}} with NJ=Mb⋅NN_{J}=M_{b}\cdot N, and defines the mm-th leave-one-out jackknife sample as OmJ=∑l≠mOlNJ−1O_{m}^{\rm{J}}=\cfrac{\sum_{l\neq m}O_{l}}{N_{J}-1} for m∈{1,…,NJ}m\in\{1,\ldots,N_{J}\}. Then, the mean and variance are computed:

μ=μJ=1NJ​∑m=1NJOmJ\mu=\mu^{J}=\cfrac{1}{N_{J}}\sum_{m=1}^{N_{J}}O_{m}^{\rm{J}} (25)

and

σ2=(NJ−1)​(σJ)2=NJ−1NJ​∑m=1NJ(OmJ−μJ)2.\sigma^{2}=(N_{J}-1)(\sigma^{J})^{2}=\cfrac{N_{J}-1}{N_{J}}\sum_{m=1}^{N_{J}}\left(O_{m}^{\rm{J}}-\mu^{\rm{J}}\right)^{2}. (26)

The jackknife (with reblocking) can also be applied to estimate the mean and variance of the accumulated weighted observables. This is needed for MCMC with the reweighting technique or for LRDMC. The weighted average is defined as O¯=∑lwl​Ol∑lwl\bar{O}=\cfrac{\sum_{l}w_{l}O_{l}}{\sum_{l}w_{l}}, with ll running over all MCMC samples. The mm-th leave-one-out jackknife sample is OmJ=∑l≠mwl​Ol∑l≠mwl=∑lwl​Ol−wm​Om∑lwl−wmO_{m}^{\rm{J}}=\cfrac{\sum_{l\neq m}w_{l}O_{l}}{\sum_{l\neq m}w_{l}}=\cfrac{\sum_{l}w_{l}O_{l}-w_{m}O_{m}}{\sum_{l}w_{l}-w_{m}}. If ℐβ\mathcal{I}_{\beta} denotes the set of MCMC step indices belonging to block β\beta, the leave-one-block-out jackknife sample is then OβJ=∑l∉ℐβwl​Ol∑l∉ℐβwl=∑lwl​Ol−∑l∈ℐβwl​Ol∑lwl−∑l∈ℐβwlO_{\beta}^{\rm{J}}=\cfrac{\sum_{l\notin\mathcal{I}_{\beta}}w_{l}O_{l}}{\sum_{l\notin\mathcal{I}_{\beta}}w_{l}}=\cfrac{\sum_{l}w_{l}O_{l}-\sum_{l\in\mathcal{I}_{\beta}}w_{l}O_{l}}{\sum_{l}w_{l}-\sum_{l\in\mathcal{I}_{\beta}}w_{l}}. Then, the mean and variance are computed in the same way for the OmJO_{m}^{\rm{J}} quantities as described by Eqs. 25 and 26, respectively.

III Wave functions

jQMC employs a many-body wavefunction ansatz Ψ\Psi composed of the Jastrow factor and the antisymmetric (AS) part:

Ψ=exp⁡(J)×ΦAS,\Psi=\exp(J)\times\Phi_{\text{AS}}\,, (27)

where exp⁡(J)\exp(J) is symmetric under electron exchange, while ΦAS\Phi_{\text{AS}} is antisymmetric. jQMC currently offers three choices of ΦAS\Phi_{\text{AS}}: (i)\rm(\hskip 1.79993pti\hskip 1.79993pt) the Antisymmetrized Geminal Power (AGP), (ii)\rm(\hskip 0.80002ptii\hskip 0.80002pt) the AGP with a constrained number of molecular orbitals (AGPn), and (iii)\rm(i\hskip-0.80002pti\hskip-0.80002pti) the single Slater determinant. In this Section, we will describe the functional form of the Jastrow factor (sec. III.1), the AGP (sec. III.2), the AGPn (sec. III.3), the SD (sec. III.4), their fast-update implementations (sec. III.5), and the basis set and atomic orbitals used in the Jastrow and AS parts (sec. III.6).

III.1 Jastrow factor

The Jastrow factor, exp⁡(J)\exp(J), is required to include electronic correlation and satisfy Kato’s cusp conditions [30]. In jQMC, the Jastrow term is written as the sum of one-body, two-body, and three- or four-body contributions: J=J1+J2+J3/4J=J_{1}+J_{2}+J_{3/4}. The one-body and two-body terms play a role in satisfying the electron-ion and electron-electron cusp conditions, respectively. The three- and four-body terms account for additional electron correlation. The one-body Jastrow factor J1J_{1} is the sum of two parts, the homogeneous part for the electron-ion cusp:

J1h​(𝐫1,…,𝐫N)=∑i=1Ne∑I=1Na(−(2​ZI)3/4​u​((2​ZI)1/4​|𝐫i−𝐑I|)),J_{1}^{\rm h}\left(\mathbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{N}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\rm{e}}}\sum_{I=1}^{N_{\text{a}}}\left({{-{{\left({2{Z_{I}}}\right)}^{3/4}}u\left({(2{Z_{I}})^{1/4}\left|{{\mathbf{r}_{i}}-{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}}\right|}\right)}}\right), (28)

and the inhomogeneous part:

J1inh​(𝐫1,…,𝐫N)=∑i=1Ne∑I=1Na(∑lLI,l​χI,l​(𝐫i)),{J_{1}^{\rm inh}}\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}},\ldots,{{\mathbf{r}}_{N}}}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\rm{e}}}\sum_{I=1}^{N_{\text{a}}}\left({\sum\limits_{l}{L_{I,l}\chi_{I,l}\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}\right)}}\right), (29)

where 𝐫i{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}} are the electron positions, 𝐑I{{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}} are the atomic positions with their atomic number ZIZ_{I}, ll runs over atomic orbitals χI,l\chi_{I,l} centered on the atom II, {LI,l}\{L_{I,l}\} are variational parameters, and u⁡(r){u\left(r\right)} is a simple bounded function. In jQMC, two functional forms are available for uu: the exponential form (default option),

uexp​(r)=12​bei​(1−e−r​bei),u^{\rm exp}\left(r\right)=\frac{1}{2b_{\text{ei}}}\left({1-{e^{-rb_{\text{ei}}}}}\right)\,, (30)

and the Padé form,

uPad​e´​(r)=r2​(1+bei​r)−1,u^{\rm Pad\acute{e}}\left(r\right)=\frac{r}{2}\left(1+b_{\text{ei}}\,r\right)^{-1}\,, (31)

both depending on a single variational parameter beib_{\text{ei}}. Both forms satisfy the electron-ion cusp condition and are bounded for r→∞r\to\infty.

The two-body Jastrow factor is defined as:

J2​(𝐫1,…,𝐫N)=∑i<jvσi,σj​(|𝐫i−𝐫j|),{J_{2}}\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}},\ldots,{{\mathbf{r}}_{N}}}\right)={\sum\limits_{i<j}{{v_{{\sigma_{i}},{\sigma_{j}}}}\left({\left|{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}-{{\mathbf{r}}_{j}}}\right|}\right)}}, (32)

where vσi,σjv_{{\sigma_{i}},{\sigma_{j}}} is another simple bounded function. In jQMC, two functional forms are implemented: the Padé form (default),

vPad​e´​(ri,j)=ri,j2​(1+bee​ri,j)−1,{v^{\rm Pad\acute{e}}}\left({{r_{i,j}}}\right)=\frac{{{r_{i,j}}}}{2}{\left({1+b_{\rm{ee}}{{r_{i,j}}}}\right)^{-1}}\,, (33)

and the exponential form,

vexp​(ri,j)=12​bee​(1−e−bee​ri,j),{v^{\rm exp}}\left({{r_{i,j}}}\right)=\frac{1}{2b_{\rm{ee}}}\left(1-e^{-b_{\rm{ee}}\,r_{i,j}}\right)\,, (34)

where ri,j=|𝐫i−𝐫j|{r_{i,j}}=\left|{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}-{{\mathbf{r}}_{j}}}\right|, and beeb_{\rm{ee}} is the variational parameter. In principle, vσi,σjv_{{\sigma_{i}},{\sigma_{j}}} depends on spin, if both like-spin and unlike-spin cusp conditions are fulfilled. In jQMC, we have implemented so far only the spin-independent version, fulfilling the electron-electron cusp conditions for opposite spins.

The three/four-body Jastrow factor reads:

J3/4​(𝐫1,…,𝐫N)=∑i<j(∑l∑l′Ml,l′​χl​(𝐫i)​χl′​(𝐫j)),J_{3/4}\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{1}},\ldots,{{\mathbf{r}}_{N}}}\right)=\sum_{i<j}\left(\sum_{l}\sum_{l^{\prime}}M_{l,l^{\prime}}\chi_{l}(\mathbf{r}_{i})\chi_{l^{\prime}}(\mathbf{r}_{j})\right), (35)

where the indices ll and l′l^{\prime} indicate different orbitals and {Ml,l′}\{M_{l,l^{\prime}}\} are variational parameters. χ\chi are Gaussian-type atomic orbitals (GTOs), described later.

III.2 Antisymmetrized Geminal Power (AGP)

jQMC implements the antisymmetrized geminal power (AGP) ansatz for the fermionic antisymmetric part of the trial wave function. The AGP ansatz was first applied to ab initio quantum Monte Carlo calculations by Casula and Sorella [14], and has since been adopted in several QMC codes. For simplicity, we first consider a system with an even number NN of electrons. The AGP wave function is written as an antisymmetrized product of two-electron geminal gg,

ΦAS(𝟏,…,𝐍)=𝒜[g(𝟏,𝟐)g(𝟑,𝟒)⋯g(𝐍−𝟏,𝐍)],\Phi_{\rm AS}(\mathbf{1},\ldots,\mathbf{N})={\cal A}\left[g(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{2})g(\mathbf{3},\mathbf{4})\cdots g(\mathbf{N-1},\mathbf{N})\right], (36)

where 𝐢≡(𝐫i,σi)\mathbf{i}\equiv(\mathbf{r}_{i},\sigma_{i}) denotes the spatial and spin coordinates of electron ii. The antisymmetrization operator is defined as

𝒜=1N!​∑P∈SNϵP​P^,{\cal A}={1\over N!}\sum_{P\in S_{N}}\epsilon_{P}\hat{P}, (37)

where SNS_{N} is the permutation group of NN elements, P^\hat{P} is the operator associated with the permutation PP, and ϵP\epsilon_{P} is the sign. Let GG be the N×NN\times N matrix whose elements are

Gi​j=g⁡(𝐢,𝐣).G_{ij}=g(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}). (38)

Because of fermionic antisymmetry, the geminal satisfies

g⁡(𝐢,𝐣)=−g⁡(𝐣,𝐢),Gi​j=−Gj​i,g(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})=-g(\mathbf{j},\mathbf{i}),\qquad G_{ij}=-G_{ji}, (39)

and hence GG is skew-symmetric. In this general spin-coordinate representation, the AGP amplitude is therefore proportional to the Pfaffian of GG. The overall proportionality factor is irrelevant for variational Monte Carlo because the wave function is used up to normalization. In the current implementation, jQMC supports only opposite-spin pairings. Although the full geminal g⁡(𝐢,𝐣)g(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}) is defined in the spin-coordinate space, only the spin up–spin down block is evaluated explicitly in the opposite-spin implementation. With the electrons ordered such that all spin-up are followed by all spin-down electrons, the full skew-symmetric geminal matrix has the block form

G=(0F−FT0),G=\begin{pmatrix}0&F\\ -F^{T}&0\end{pmatrix}, (40)

where

Fi​j=f⁡(𝐫i↑,𝐫j↓).F_{ij}=f(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\uparrow},\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\downarrow}). (41)

The spin down–spin up block is therefore fixed by antisymmetry and does not need to be computed independently. For Ne↑=Ne↓N_{e}^{\uparrow}=N_{e}^{\downarrow}, the Pfaffian of GG is proportional to detF\det F, and the irrelevant overall sign is absorbed in the normalization convention. Thus, jQMC evaluates only the determinant of the spin up–spin down pairing matrix FF:

ΦAS​(𝐱↑,𝐱↓)=detF,\Phi_{\rm AS}(\mathbf{x}^{\uparrow},\mathbf{x}^{\downarrow})=\det F, (42)

where 𝐱↑=(𝐫1↑,…,𝐫N↑↑)\mathbf{x}^{\uparrow}=(\mathbf{r}_{1}^{\uparrow},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{N_{\uparrow}}^{\uparrow}) and 𝐱↓=(𝐫1↓,…,𝐫N↓↓)\mathbf{x}^{\downarrow}=(\mathbf{r}_{1}^{\downarrow},\ldots,\mathbf{r}_{N_{\downarrow}}^{\downarrow}), with the matrix FF defined in Eq. 41. The spatial pairing function is expanded on a chosen one-particle basis as

f⁡(𝐫i↑,𝐫j↓)=∑l​mΛl​m↑⁣↓​ψl↑​(𝐫i↑)​ψm↓​(𝐫j↓),f(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\uparrow},\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\downarrow})=\sum_{lm}\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}_{lm}\psi_{l}^{\uparrow}(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\uparrow})\psi_{m}^{\downarrow}(\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\downarrow}), (43)

where Λ↑⁣↓\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow} is the geminal coefficient matrix in the chosen orbital basis. The orbitals ψl↑\psi_{l}^{\uparrow} and ψm↓\psi_{m}^{\downarrow} can be either atomic or molecular. The spin character of the pair is especially transparent when the spatial orbitals are spin independent,

ψl↑​(𝐫)=ψl↓​(𝐫)≡ψl​(𝐫).\psi_{l}^{\uparrow}(\mathbf{r})=\psi_{l}^{\downarrow}(\mathbf{r})\equiv\psi_{l}(\mathbf{r}). (44)

In this case, the opposite-spin geminal can be written as

g⁡(𝐢,𝐣)=f⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)​χ↑​(σi)​χ↓​(σj)−f⁡(𝐫j,𝐫i)​χ↓​(σi)​χ↑​(σj).g(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})=f(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j})\chi_{\uparrow}(\sigma_{i})\chi_{\downarrow}(\sigma_{j})-f(\mathbf{r}_{j},\mathbf{r}_{i})\chi_{\downarrow}(\sigma_{i})\chi_{\uparrow}(\sigma_{j}). (45)

Introducing the symmetric and skew-symmetric parts of the spatial pairing function,

fS​(𝐫i,𝐫j)\displaystyle f_{S}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j}) =12​[f⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)+f⁡(𝐫j,𝐫i)],\displaystyle={1\over 2}\left[f(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j})+f(\mathbf{r}_{j},\mathbf{r}_{i})\right], (46)
fA​(𝐫i,𝐫j)\displaystyle f_{A}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j}) =12​[f⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)−f⁡(𝐫j,𝐫i)],\displaystyle={1\over 2}\left[f(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j})-f(\mathbf{r}_{j},\mathbf{r}_{i})\right], (47)

the geminal becomes

g⁡(𝐢,𝐣)=\displaystyle g(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j})= fS​(𝐫i,𝐫j)​[χ↑​(σi)​χ↓​(σj)−χ↓​(σi)​χ↑​(σj)]\displaystyle\;f_{S}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j})\left[\chi_{\uparrow}(\sigma_{i})\chi_{\downarrow}(\sigma_{j})-\chi_{\downarrow}(\sigma_{i})\chi_{\uparrow}(\sigma_{j})\right]
+fA​(𝐫i,𝐫j)​[χ↑​(σi)​χ↓​(σj)+χ↓​(σi)​χ↑​(σj)].\displaystyle+f_{A}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j})\left[\chi_{\uparrow}(\sigma_{i})\chi_{\downarrow}(\sigma_{j})+\chi_{\downarrow}(\sigma_{i})\chi_{\uparrow}(\sigma_{j})\right]. (48)

Thus, the symmetric part of the spatial pairing function is associated with a spin-singlet pair, whereas the skew-symmetric part is associated with the MS=0M_{S}=0 component of a spin-triplet pair. Equivalently, when the same spin-independent orbital basis is used for both spins, the decomposition is controlled by

Λ↑⁣↓=ΛS+ΛA,ΛS=12​[Λ↑⁣↓+(Λ↑⁣↓)T],ΛA=12​[Λ↑⁣↓−(Λ↑⁣↓)T].\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}=\Lambda^{S}+\Lambda^{A},\qquad\Lambda^{S}={1\over 2}\left[\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}+(\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow})^{T}\right],\qquad\Lambda^{A}={1\over 2}\left[\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}-(\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow})^{T}\right]. (49)

A symmetric Λ↑⁣↓\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow} therefore gives a singlet AGP component, while a skew-symmetric Λ↑⁣↓\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow} gives the MS=0M_{S}=0 triplet AGP component. A general matrix Λ↑⁣↓\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow} contains both components. jQMC preserves a given symmetry of the geminal matrix during the WF optimization.

The AGP ansatz can also be generalized to spin-polarized systems. Without loss of generality, we can assume Ne↑>Ne↓N_{e}^{\uparrow}>N_{e}^{\downarrow} and the system contains Ne↓N_{e}^{\downarrow} opposite-spin pairs with k=Ne↑−Ne↓k=N_{e}^{\uparrow}-N_{e}^{\downarrow} unpaired spin-up electrons. In this case, the determinant form is obtained by concatenating the spin up–spin down pairing matrix with kk unpaired orbitals:

ΦAS=detF~,\Phi_{\rm AS}=\det\tilde{F}, (50)

where

F~=[F↑⁣↓|U↑].\tilde{F}=\left[F^{\uparrow\downarrow}\;\middle|\;U^{\uparrow}\right]. (51)

Here, F↑⁣↓F^{\uparrow\downarrow} is an Ne↑×Ne↓N_{e}^{\uparrow}\times N_{e}^{\downarrow} matrix describing opposite-spin pairings, and U↑U^{\uparrow} is an Ne↑×kN_{e}^{\uparrow}\times k matrix describing the unpaired orbitals. Explicitly,

Fi​j↑⁣↓\displaystyle F^{\uparrow\downarrow}_{ij} =∑l​mΛl​m↑⁣↓​ψl↑​(𝐫i↑)​ψm↓​(𝐫j↓),\displaystyle=\sum_{lm}\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}_{lm}\psi_{l}^{\uparrow}(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\uparrow})\psi_{m}^{\downarrow}(\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\downarrow}), (52)
Ui​a↑\displaystyle U^{\uparrow}_{ia} =∑lΛl​a↑ψl↑(𝐫i↑),a=1,…,k.\displaystyle=\sum_{l}\Lambda^{\uparrow}_{la}\psi_{l}^{\uparrow}(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\uparrow}),\qquad a=1,\ldots,k. (53)

The resulting matrix F~\tilde{F} is square, with dimension Ne↑×Ne↑N_{e}^{\uparrow}\times N_{e}^{\uparrow}, and its determinant gives the antisymmetric part of the wave function for the spin-polarized system.

We now describe the matrix form used in the implementation. Let Ψ↑\Psi^{\uparrow} and Ψ↓\Psi^{\downarrow} be the orbital-value matrices,

Ψl​i↑=ψl↑​(𝐫i↑),Ψm​j↓=ψm↓​(𝐫j↓).\Psi^{\uparrow}_{li}=\psi_{l}^{\uparrow}(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\uparrow}),\qquad\Psi^{\downarrow}_{mj}=\psi_{m}^{\downarrow}(\mathbf{r}_{j}^{\downarrow}). (54)

For an atomic orbital (AO) basis of size Na​oN_{ao}, the dimensions of these matrices are (Na​oN_{ao}, Ne↑N_{e}^{\uparrow}) and (Na​oN_{ao}, Ne↓N_{e}^{\downarrow}), respectively. The paired block is assembled as a matrix–matrix product,

F↑⁣↓=(Ψ↑)T​Λ↑⁣↓​Ψ↓,F^{\uparrow\downarrow}=(\Psi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}\Psi^{\downarrow}, (55)

where Λ↑⁣↓\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow} has dimension (Na​oN_{ao}, Na​oN_{ao}). The unpaired block is similarly written as

U↑=(Ψ↑)T​Λ↑,U^{\uparrow}=(\Psi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda^{\uparrow}, (56)

where Λ↑\Lambda^{\uparrow} has dimension (Na​oN_{ao}, kk). Therefore,

F~=[(Ψ↑)T​Λ↑⁣↓​Ψ↓|(Ψ↑)T​Λ↑].\tilde{F}=\left[(\Psi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}\Psi^{\downarrow}\;\middle|\;(\Psi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda^{\uparrow}\right]. (57)

For convenience, the variational parameters may be stored as the concatenated matrix

Λ~=[Λ↑⁣↓|Λ↑],\tilde{\Lambda}=\left[\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow}\;\middle|\;\Lambda^{\uparrow}\right], (58)

whose dimension is (MM, M+kM+k). The first MM columns define the opposite-spin pairing block, while the remaining kk columns define the unpaired orbitals.

The same formalism applies whether the orbital basis is chosen to be AOs or molecular orbitals (MOs). Let Ψσ\Psi^{\sigma} denote the AO-value matrix and Φσ\Phi^{\sigma} the MO-value matrix for spin σ\sigma. We use the convention

Φ↑=C↑​Ψ↑,Φ↓=C↓​Ψ↓,\Phi^{\uparrow}=C^{\uparrow}\Psi^{\uparrow},\qquad\Phi^{\downarrow}=C^{\downarrow}\Psi^{\downarrow}, (59)

where C↑C^{\uparrow} and C↓C^{\downarrow} are the MO coefficient matrices, whose dimensions are (Nm​o↑N_{mo}^{\uparrow}, Na​oN_{ao}) and (Nm​o↓N_{mo}^{\downarrow}, Na​oN_{ao}), respectively. In spin-polarized calculations, the MO coefficients may differ between the two spin sectors. If ΛM↑⁣↓\Lambda_{M}^{\uparrow\downarrow} and ΛM↑\Lambda_{M}^{\uparrow} are the geminal and unpaired-orbital coefficient matrices in the MO representation, respectively, the corresponding AO representation is

ΛA↑⁣↓\displaystyle\Lambda_{A}^{\uparrow\downarrow} =(C↑)T​ΛM↑⁣↓​C↓,\displaystyle=(C^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda_{M}^{\uparrow\downarrow}C^{\downarrow}, (60)
ΛA↑\displaystyle\Lambda_{A}^{\uparrow} =(C↑)T​ΛM↑.\displaystyle=(C^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda_{M}^{\uparrow}. (61)

With these definitions, the concatenated pairing matrix is invariant under the AO–MO transformation:

F~AO\displaystyle\tilde{F}^{\rm AO} =[(Ψ↑)T​ΛA↑⁣↓​Ψ↓|(Ψ↑)T​ΛA↑],\displaystyle=\left[(\Psi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda_{A}^{\uparrow\downarrow}\Psi^{\downarrow}\;\middle|\;(\Psi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda_{A}^{\uparrow}\right], (62)
F~MO\displaystyle\tilde{F}^{\rm MO} =[(Φ↑)T​ΛM↑⁣↓​Φ↓|(Φ↑)T​ΛM↑],\displaystyle=\left[(\Phi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda_{M}^{\uparrow\downarrow}\Phi^{\downarrow}\;\middle|\;(\Phi^{\uparrow})^{T}\Lambda_{M}^{\uparrow}\right], (63)
F~AO\displaystyle\tilde{F}^{\rm AO} =F~MO.\displaystyle=\tilde{F}^{\rm MO}. (64)

Thus, the AGP wave functions expanded in AOs and MOs are evaluated by the same matrix operations in jQMC.

III.3 AGP with constrained number of molecular orbital (AGPn)

If one expands the AGP pairing function with molecular orbitals, and neglects the non-diagonal terms of the pairing matrix or diagonalizes the pairing function to express it as a function of AGP natural orbitals, the resultant pairing function reads:

𝐅~M​O​(𝐱↑,𝐱↓)=[(𝚽↑)T​𝚲M,diag↑,↓​𝚽↓|(𝚽↑)T​𝚲M↑],\tilde{\mathbf{F}}^{MO}(\mathbf{x}^{\uparrow},\mathbf{x}^{\downarrow})=[(\bm{\Phi}^{\uparrow})^{T}\bm{\Lambda}_{M,{\rm diag}}^{\uparrow,\downarrow}\bm{\Phi}^{\downarrow}|(\bm{\Phi}^{\uparrow})^{T}\bm{\Lambda}_{M}^{\uparrow}], (65)

where ΛM,diag↑,↓\Lambda_{M,{\rm diag}}^{\uparrow,\downarrow} is the diagonal matrix (i.e., the non-diagonal terms are set to zero, neglecting couplings between different MO indices). This is what we call the AGPn ansatz.

III.4 Single Slater determinant (SD)

The AGP ansatz is reduced to the Slater Determinant if one restricts Mm​o=Ne↑M_{mo}=N_{e}^{\uparrow} or, equivalently, if the rank of the Λ↑,↓\Lambda^{\uparrow,\downarrow} matrix is equal to Ne↓N_{e}^{\downarrow}, with Ne↑−Ne↓N_{e}^{\uparrow}-N_{e}^{\downarrow} independent MOs. In this limit, we can neglect the non-diagonal elements of Λ↑,↓\Lambda^{\uparrow,\downarrow} and Λ↑\Lambda^{\uparrow}, i.e., λi,j↑,↓=δi,j\lambda_{i,j}^{\uparrow,\downarrow}=\delta_{i,j} (dim.: Ne↓,Ne↓N^{\downarrow}_{e},N^{\downarrow}_{e}) and λl,k↑=δl,k+Ne↓\lambda_{l,k}^{\uparrow}=\delta_{l,k+N_{e}^{\downarrow}} (dim: Ne↑,Ne↑−Ne↓N_{e}^{\uparrow},N_{e}^{\uparrow}-N_{e}^{\downarrow}). A typical starting point of a VMC calculation from HF/DFT is the SD anstaz with randomized (or zero) Jastrow factor parameters.

III.5 Fast update of wave function

jQMC employs a single-electron move algorithm in MCMC, where only one electron position is updated in each proposed MCMC step. The same single-electron update is also used in LRDMC, as the algorithm requires. Furthermore, both MCMC and LRDMC require evaluating the wave function at specific spatial grid points for the non-local ECP term and for the discretized kinetic-energy operator (LRDMC only). These evaluations involve moving only one electron at the time from the original electron configuration. In such cases, one does not need to evaluate the wave function with all electron coordinates from scratch, but one needs just to compute its variation through the single-electron move. In this situation, one should exploit the so-called fast-update technique to drastically save the computational cost for both the Jastrow factor and determinant parts. More specifically, MCMC or LRDMC requires the evaluation of the wave function ratio Ψ⁡(𝐱′)/Ψ⁡(𝐱)\Psi(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})/\Psi(\mathbf{x}). The ratio is decomposed into the determinant part D⁡(𝐱′)/D⁡(𝐱)D(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})/D(\mathbf{x}) and eJ⁡(𝐱′)/eJ⁡(𝐱)e^{J(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})}/e^{J(\mathbf{x})}, and computed separately.

The Jastrow ratio is computed as eJ⁡(𝐱′)/eJ⁡(𝐱)≡eΔ​Je^{J(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})}/e^{J(\mathbf{x})}\equiv e^{\Delta J}, where Δ​J=J⁡(𝐱′)−J⁡(𝐱)\Delta J=J(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})-J(\mathbf{x}). Most contributions to JJ cancel exactly since only a single electron has been moved. As already described in Sec. III.1, the Jastrow factor is made of three different terms. Each of them requires a different implementation for fast updates.

For the determinant ratio, let F~old\tilde{F}^{\rm old} be the spatial pairing matrix [the same F~\tilde{F} as in Eq. (51)] before a proposed move and F~new\tilde{F}^{\rm new} the matrix after updating electron ll. A single-electron move modifies only one row or one column of F~\tilde{F}: a spin-up move updates row ll, whereas a spin-down move updates column ll. Therefore, the new matrix can always be written as a rank-1 update,

F~new=F~old+𝐮l​𝐯lT,\tilde{F}^{\rm new}=\tilde{F}^{\rm old}+\mathbf{u}_{l}\mathbf{v}_{l}^{T}, (66)

with

(𝐮l,𝐯l)={(𝐞l,[F~newl,:−F~oldl,:]T),spin-up move,(F~new:,l−F~old:,l,𝐞l),spin-down move,(\mathbf{u}_{l},\mathbf{v}_{l})=\begin{cases}\left(\mathbf{e}_{l},\;[\tilde{F}^{\rm new}_{l,:}-\tilde{F}^{\rm old}_{l,:}]^{T}\right),&\text{spin-up move},\\[2.84526pt] \left(\tilde{F}^{\rm new}_{:,l}-\tilde{F}^{\rm old}_{:,l},\;\mathbf{e}_{l}\right),&\text{spin-down move},\end{cases} (67)

where 𝐞l\mathbf{e}_{l} is the ll-th Cartesian basis vector. The Slater determinant is treated in the same way, since the single-determinant ansatz is a special case of AGP. Using the matrix determinant lemma,

det[F~new]=det[F~old+𝐮l​𝐯lT]=(1+𝐯lT​(F~old)−1​𝐮l)​det[F~old],\det[\tilde{F}^{\rm new}]=\det[\tilde{F}^{\rm old}+\mathbf{u}_{l}\mathbf{v}_{l}^{T}]=\left(1+\mathbf{v}_{l}^{T}(\tilde{F}^{\rm old})^{-1}\mathbf{u}_{l}\right)\det[\tilde{F}^{\rm old}], (68)

and thus the determinant ratio is

ρdet≡det[F~new]det[F~old]=1+𝐯lT​(F~old)−1​𝐮l.\rho_{\rm det}\equiv\frac{\det[\tilde{F}^{\rm new}]}{\det[\tilde{F}^{\rm old}]}=1+\mathbf{v}_{l}^{T}(\tilde{F}^{\rm old})^{-1}\mathbf{u}_{l}. (69)

Thus, the acceptance ratio can be evaluated without recomputing det[F~new]\det[\tilde{F}^{\rm new}] from scratch. After an accepted move, the inverse matrix is updated using the Sherman-Morrison formula,

(F~new)−1=(F~old+𝐮l​𝐯lT)−1=(F~old)−1−(F~old)−1​𝐮l​(1+𝐯lT​(F~old)−1​𝐮l)−1​𝐯lT​(F~old)−1.(\tilde{F}^{\rm new})^{-1}=(\tilde{F}^{\rm old}+\mathbf{u}_{l}\mathbf{v}_{l}^{T})^{-1}=(\tilde{F}^{\rm old})^{-1}-(\tilde{F}^{\rm old})^{-1}\mathbf{u}_{l}\left(1+\mathbf{v}_{l}^{T}(\tilde{F}^{\rm old})^{-1}\mathbf{u}_{l}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{v}_{l}^{T}(\tilde{F}^{\rm old})^{-1}. (70)

The cost of this standard procedure is dominated by matrix-vector operations. To reduce this overhead, McDaniel et al. [37] proposed the delayed-update scheme, but this is not yet implemented in jQMC.

III.6 Atomic orbitals for the pairing function and the Jastrow factor

One of the most common choices for atomic orbitals is atom-centered Gaussian-type orbitals, denoted as GTOs. A GTO is composed of the radial and angular parts. There are two conventions for the angular part: One is the solid harmonics, and the other is the polynomial functions in the Cartesian basis. jQMC implements both of them.

III.6.1 Gaussian-Type Atomic orbitals with Solid-harmonics basis functions

Primitive atomic orbitals (ψl,m,I​(𝐫)\psi_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r})) with the (regular) solid harmonic basis functions are given in the following Gaussian form:

ψl,m,I​(𝐫)=𝒩l,m,Isolid​ℛI​(𝐫)​𝒮l,m,I​(𝐫),\psi_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r})=\mathcal{N}^{\rm solid}_{l,m,I}\mathcal{R}_{I}(\mathbf{r})\mathcal{S}_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r}), (71)

which can be evaluated using Cartesian coordinates (i.e., x,y,zx,y,z) because there is no singular point, where the radial part and solid harmonics are defined as:

ℛI(𝐫)=e−ZI⋅|𝐑I−𝐫|2,\mathcal{R}_{I}(\mathbf{r})=e^{-Z_{I}\cdot|\mathbf{R}_{I}-\mathbf{r}|^{2}}, (72)

and

𝒮l,m,I​(𝐫)=2​l+14​π⋅|𝐑I−𝐫|l⋅𝒴l,m​(θI,ϕI),\mathcal{S}_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r})=\sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}}\cdot|\mathbf{R}_{I}-\mathbf{r}|^{l}\cdot\mathcal{Y}_{l,m}(\theta_{I},\phi_{I}), (73)

where 2​l+14​π\sqrt{\cfrac{2l+1}{4\pi}} in 𝒮l,m,I​(𝐫)\mathcal{S}_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r}) is the Racah’s normalization factor for the solid harmonics part, resulting in ∫0π∫02​πsin⁡θ​𝑑θ​𝑑ϕ​𝒮l,m,I∗​(𝐫)​𝒮l,m,I​(𝐫)=4​π2​l+1​r2​l\int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin\theta d\theta d\phi\mathcal{S}_{l,m,I}^{*}(\mathbf{r})\mathcal{S}_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r})=\cfrac{4\pi}{2l+1}r^{2l}. The normalization factor, 𝒩l,m,Isolid\mathcal{N}^{\rm solid}_{l,m,I}, is defined as

𝒩l,Isolid=(2​ZI/π)3/2​(4​ZI)l(2​l−1)!!.\mathcal{N}_{l,I}^{\rm{solid}}=\sqrt{\frac{(2Z_{I}/\pi)^{3/2}(4Z_{I})^{l}}{(2l-1)!!}}. (74)

The GTO can also be written with real spherical harmonics as:

ψl,m,I​(𝐫)=𝒩l,m,Isphe⋅|𝐑I−𝐫|l⋅ℛI​(𝐫)⋅𝒴l,m​(θI,ϕI),\psi_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r})=\mathcal{N}_{l,m,I}^{\rm{sphe}}\cdot|\mathbf{R}_{I}-\mathbf{r}|^{l}\cdot\mathcal{R}_{I}(\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathcal{Y}_{l,m}(\theta_{I},\phi_{I}), (75)

where θI\theta_{I} and ϕI\phi_{I} are polar (0≤θ<π0\leq\theta<\pi) and azimuthal (0≤ϕ<2​π0\leq\phi<2\pi) angles in the spherical coordinate whose origin is 𝐑I\mathbf{R}_{I}, 𝒴l,m​(θ,ϕ)\mathcal{Y}_{l,m}(\theta,\phi) is the real spherical harmonics, and 𝒩l,Isphe\mathcal{N}^{\rm sphe}_{l,I} is the normalization factor:

𝒩l,Isphe=22​l+3​(l+1)!​(2​ZI)l+32(2​l+2)!​π.\mathcal{N}^{\rm sphe}_{l,I}=\sqrt{\frac{2^{2l+3}(l+1)!(2Z_{I})^{l+\frac{3}{2}}}{(2l+2)!\sqrt{\pi}}}. (76)

Notice that the relation between the normalizations factors is 𝒩l,m,Isolid𝒩l,m,Isphe=2​l+14​π\cfrac{\mathcal{N}^{\rm solid}_{l,m,I}}{\mathcal{N}^{\rm sphe}_{l,m,I}}=\sqrt{\cfrac{2l+1}{4\pi}}.

III.6.2 Gaussian-Type Atomic orbitals with Cartesian basis functions

Primitive atomic orbitals (ψl,m,I​(𝐫)\psi_{l,m,I}(\mathbf{r})) with Cartesian basis functions are given in the following Gaussian form:

ψnx,ny,nz,I(𝐫)=𝒩nx,ny,nz,Icart⋅e−ZI⋅|𝐑I−𝐫|2⋅𝒫nx,ny,nz(x,y,z),\psi_{n_{x},n_{y},n_{z},I}(\mathbf{r})=\mathcal{N}_{n_{x},n_{y},n_{z},I}^{\rm{cart}}\cdot e^{-Z_{I}\cdot|\mathbf{R}_{I}-\mathbf{r}|^{2}}\cdot\mathcal{P}_{n_{x},n_{y},n_{z}}(x,y,z), (77)

where 𝒫nx,ny,nz​(x,y,z)=xnx​yny​xnz\mathcal{P}_{n_{x},n_{y},n_{z}}(x,y,z)=x^{n_{x}}y^{n_{y}}x^{n_{z}}, 𝒩nx,ny,nz,Icart\mathcal{N}_{n_{x},n_{y},n_{z},I}^{\rm{cart}} is the normalization factor for an orbital (nx,ny,nz,I)(n_{x},n_{y},n_{z},I) discussed later. The normalization 𝒩nx,ny,nz,Icart\mathcal{N}_{n_{x},n_{y},n_{z},I}^{\rm{cart}} is computed as:

𝒩nx,ny,nz,Icart=(2​ZI/π)3/2​(4​ZI)nx+ny+nz(2​nx−1)!!​(2​ny−1)!!​(2​nz−1)!!≡(2​ZI/π)3/2​(8​ZI)nx+ny+nz​nx!​ny!​nz!(2​nx)!​(2​ny)!​(2​nz)!.\mathcal{N}_{n_{x},n_{y},n_{z},I}^{\rm{cart}}=\sqrt{\frac{(2Z_{I}/\pi)^{3/2}(4Z_{I})^{n_{x}+n_{y}+n_{z}}}{(2n_{x}-1)!!(2n_{y}-1)!!(2n_{z}-1)!!}}\equiv\sqrt{\cfrac{(2Z_{I}/\pi)^{3/2}(8Z_{I})^{n_{x}+n_{y}+n_{z}}n_{x}!n_{y}!n_{z}!}{(2n_{x})!(2n_{y})!(2n_{z})!}}. (78)

The total angular momentum ll is defined as l=nx+ny+nzl=n_{x}+n_{y}+n_{z}. jQMC stores the polynomial functions in the canonical (or alphabetical) ordering, as in TREX-IO [62], e.g., l=0→sl=0\rightarrow s, l=1→px,py,pzl=1\rightarrow p_{x},p_{y},p_{z}, l=2→dx​x,dx​y,dx​z,dy​y,dy​z,dz​zl=2\rightarrow d_{xx},d_{xy},d_{xz},d_{yy},d_{yz},d_{zz}. Notice that the above equation implies that the normalization factor is not common for all orbitals with the same ll except for ss and pp orbitals. For instance, for dx​xd_{xx} and dx​yd_{xy} orbitals,

𝒩2,0,0,Icart=(2​ZI/π)3/2​(4​ZI)23,\mathcal{N}_{2,0,0,I}^{\rm{cart}}=\sqrt{\frac{(2Z_{I}/\pi)^{3/2}(4Z_{I})^{2}}{3}}, (79)

while

𝒩1,1,0,Icart=(2​ZI/π)3/2​(4​ZI)2.\mathcal{N}_{1,1,0,I}^{\rm{cart}}=\sqrt{(2Z_{I}/\pi)^{3/2}(4Z_{I})^{2}}. (80)

IV Coulomb interaction and Effective Core Potential

The potential term is decomposed into two parts, bare Coulomb interactions and effective core potential parts, V⁡(𝐱)=Vbare​(𝐱)+Vecp​(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x})=V^{\rm bare}(\mathbf{x})+V^{\rm ecp}(\mathbf{x}). The bare Coulomb part is further decomposed into three components. i.e., Vbare​(𝐱)=Vei​(𝐱)+Vee​(𝐱)+Vii​(𝐱)V^{\rm bare}(\mathbf{x})=V^{\rm ei}(\mathbf{x})+V^{\rm ee}(\mathbf{x})+V^{\rm ii}(\mathbf{x}). They are:

Vei(𝐱)=−∑l,IZI|𝐫l−𝐑I|,\displaystyle V^{\rm ei}(\mathbf{x})=-\sum_{l,I}\frac{Z_{I}}{|\mathbf{r}_{l}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|}, (81)
Vee​(𝐱)=∑l′>l1|𝐫l−𝐫l′|,\displaystyle V^{\rm ee}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{l^{\prime}>l}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_{l}-\mathbf{r}_{l^{\prime}}|}, (82)
Vii​(𝐱)=∑I′>IZI′​ZI|𝐑I′−𝐑I|.\displaystyle V^{\rm ii}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{I^{\prime}>I}\frac{Z_{I^{\prime}}Z_{I}}{|\mathbf{R}_{I^{\prime}}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|}. (83)

Notice that the electron-ion potential is often computed with semi-local potentials when ECPs are employed. In the latter case, the atomic number ZIZ_{I} is replaced by the effective charge, or pseudoatomic number, ZIeffZ^{\rm eff}_{I}, such that the electron-ion potential reads Vei(𝐱)=−∑l,IZIeff/|𝐫l−𝐑I|V^{\rm ei}(\mathbf{x})=-\sum_{l,I}Z^{\rm eff}_{I}/|\mathbf{r}_{l}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|. Nevertheless, in jQMC the electron-ion potential is separated from the semi-local potential part for the sake of clarity. Thus, Vbare​(𝐱)V^{\rm bare}(\mathbf{x}) is defined for both all-electron and ECP cases, with ZIZ_{I} replaced by ZIeffZ^{\rm eff}_{I} in Eqs. 81 and 83 if ECP are used.

In the presence of ECPs, one should treat their non-local contributions. The semi-local effective core potential is usually employed in QMC calculations, which for nucleus II is parametrized as follows:

V^ecpi,I=V^eloci,I+∑l=0lmaxV^li,I​P^li,I,\hat{V}_{\rm{ecp}}^{i,I}=\hat{V}_{\rm{eloc}}^{i,I}+\sum_{l=0}^{l_{\rm{max}}}\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}, (84)

where ii and II are electron and nucleus indices, P^li,I=∑m=−ll|Yl​m⟩i,I​⟨Yl​m|i,I\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}=\sum_{m=-l}^{l}|Y_{lm}\rangle_{i,I}\langle Y_{lm}|_{i,I} projects the angular part of electron ii’s coordinates relative to nucleus II onto the angular momentum ll, and Veloci,IV^{i,I}_{\rm eloc}, Vli,IV^{i,I}_{l} are radial functions of ri,I≡|𝐫i−𝐑I|r_{i,I}\equiv|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|. Both V^eloci,I≡VelocI​(𝐫i)\hat{V}_{\rm{eloc}}^{i,I}\equiv V_{\rm{eloc}}^{I}(\mathbf{r}_{i}) and V^li,I≡VlI​(𝐫i)\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\equiv V_{l}^{I}(\mathbf{r}_{i}) are parametrized with three parameters, aa, bb, and nn:

VelocI​(𝐫i)=1|𝐫i−𝐑I|2​∑kNIaI,k⋅|𝐫i−𝐑I|nI,k​exp⁡(−bI,k​|𝐫i−𝐑I|2),\displaystyle V_{\rm{eloc}}^{I}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{2}}\sum_{k}^{N_{I}}a_{I,k}\cdot|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{n_{I,k}}\exp(-b_{I,k}|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{2}), (85)
VlI​(𝐫i)=1|𝐫i−𝐑I|2​∑kNI,laI,k,l⋅|𝐫i−𝐑I|nI,k,l​exp⁡(−bI,k,l​|𝐫i−𝐑I|2),\displaystyle V_{l}^{I}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{2}}\sum_{k}^{N_{I,l}}a_{I,k,l}\cdot|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{n_{I,k,l}}\exp(-b_{I,k,l}|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{2}), (86)

where NIN_{I} and NI,lN_{I,l} are the number of ECP terms of the local contribution and the non-local part with angular momentum ll for nucleus II, respectively. Following the standard treatment of the semi-local form [26, 41, 8, 15], the action of V^li,I​P^li,I\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I} on a many-body wave function Ψ\Psi reduces to an angular integration at fixed electron-nucleus distance ri,Ir_{i,I}:

⟨x|V^li,I​P^li,I|Ψ⟩⟨x|Ψ⟩\displaystyle\frac{\braket{x|\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}|\Psi}}{\braket{x|\Psi}} =\displaystyle= ∫d​𝐱′​⟨x|V^li,I​P^li,I|x′⟩​⟨x′|Ψ⟩⟨x|Ψ⟩\displaystyle\int d\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\braket{x|\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}|x^{\prime}}\frac{\braket{x^{\prime}|\Psi}}{\braket{x|\Psi}} (87)
=\displaystyle= Vli,I​(ri,I)​∑m=−llYl​m​(Ωi,I)​∫d​Ωi,I′​Yl​m∗​(Ωi,I′)​Ψ⁡(…,𝐫i′,…)Ψ⁡(…,𝐫i,…)\displaystyle V_{l}^{\,i,I}(r_{i,I})\sum_{m=-l}^{l}Y_{lm}(\Omega_{i,I})\int d\Omega_{i,I}^{\prime}\;Y_{lm}^{*}(\Omega_{i,I}^{\prime})\,\frac{\Psi(\dots,\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\prime},\dots)}{\Psi(\dots,\mathbf{r}_{i},\dots)} (88)
=\displaystyle= Vli,I​(ri,I)​2​l+14​π​∫d​Ωi,I′​Pl​(𝐬i,I⋅𝐬i,I′)​Ψ⁡(…,𝐫i′,…)Ψ⁡(…,𝐫i,…),\displaystyle V_{l}^{\,i,I}(r_{i,I})\,\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}\int d\Omega_{i,I}^{\prime}\;P_{l}\!\left(\mathbf{s}_{i,I}\cdot\mathbf{s}^{\prime}_{i,I}\right)\,\frac{\Psi(\dots,\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\prime},\dots)}{\Psi(\dots,\mathbf{r}_{i},\dots)}, (89)

where 𝐬i,I≡𝐫i−𝐑I|𝐫i−𝐑I|\mathbf{s}_{i,I}\equiv\cfrac{\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|} and 𝐬i,I′≡𝐫i′−𝐑I|𝐫i′−𝐑I|\mathbf{s}^{\prime}_{i,I}\equiv\cfrac{\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\prime}-\mathbf{R}_{I}}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}^{\prime}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|}. The last identity of the above equation follows from a well-known property of the spherical harmonics [26], called the addition theorem, ∑m=−llYl​m​(Ω)​Yl​m∗​(Ω′)=2​l+14​π​Pl​(𝐬i,I⋅𝐬i,I′)\sum_{m=-l}^{l}Y_{lm}(\Omega)\,Y_{lm}^{*}(\Omega^{\prime})=\cfrac{2l+1}{4\pi}\,P_{l}(\mathbf{s}_{i,I}\cdot\mathbf{s}^{\prime}_{i,I}) where Pl​(z)P_{l}(z) is the ll-th Legendre polynomial.

jQMC implements the integration scheme proposed in Ref. 41 to perform a numerical quadrature with tetrahedrical (NV=4N_{V}=4), octahedrical (NV=6N_{V}=6, NV=18N_{V}=18), or icosahedrical (NV=12N_{V}=12) symmetry. The quadrature meshes are defined as 𝐑I+𝜹m⋅|𝐫i−𝐑I|\mathbf{R}_{I}+\bm{\delta}_{m}\cdot|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|. Since the numerical quadrature is not exact for a general wave function, the direction of zz axis of the spherical coordinate is selected randomly, θ\theta (∈[0,π[\in[0,\pi[) and ϕ\phi (∈[0,2π[\in[0,2\pi[) are selected randomly, to mitigate the bias. With the mesh, the projection is rewritten as a sum of NVN_{V} terms:

⟨x|V^li,I​P^li,I|Ψ⟩⟨x|Ψ⟩\displaystyle\frac{\braket{x|\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}|\Psi}}{\braket{x|\Psi}} =\displaystyle= ∫d​𝐱′​⟨x|V^li,I​P^li,I|x′⟩​⟨x′|Ψ⟩⟨x|Ψ⟩\displaystyle\int d\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\braket{x|\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}|x^{\prime}}\frac{\braket{x^{\prime}|\Psi}}{\braket{x|\Psi}} (90)
∼\displaystyle\sim ∑m=1Nv⟨x|V^li,I​P^li,I|xm⟩​⟨xm|Ψ⟩⟨x|Ψ⟩\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{N_{v}}\braket{x|\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}|x_{m}}\frac{\braket{x_{m}|\Psi}}{\braket{x|\Psi}} (91)
=\displaystyle= ∑m=1Nv(2​l+1)⋅Vli,I​(ri,I)⋅wm⋅Pl​(𝐬i,I⋅𝚫m)​Ψ⁡(⋯,𝐑I+𝜹m⋅|𝐫i−𝐑I|,⋯)Ψ(⋯𝐫i⋯),\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^{N_{v}}(2l+1)\cdot V_{l}^{\,i,I}(r_{i,I})\cdot w_{m}\cdot P_{l}\left(\mathbf{s}_{i,I}\cdot\bm{\Delta}_{m}\right)\frac{\Psi(\cdots,\mathbf{R}_{I}+\bm{\delta}_{m}\cdot|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|,\cdots)}{\Psi(\cdots\mathbf{r}_{i}\cdots)}, (92)

where ama_{m} are the weights of the quadrature, and 𝜹m\bm{\delta}^{m} are the points of the mesh, and 𝚫m\bm{\Delta}_{m} is the normalized one: 𝚫m≡𝜹m/|𝜹m|\bm{\Delta}_{m}\equiv\bm{\delta}_{m}/|\bm{\delta}_{m}|. The grid points are tabulated in Ref. 41, which are hard-coded in jQMC. The WF ratios on the grid points are efficiently computed via the fast-update algorithm, described in Sec. III.5, which is critically important for a fast computation for both MCMC and GFMC.

The non-local contribution arising from the application of non-local operators is naturally considered in GFMC, and more specifically in LRDMC. Indeed, in the LRDMC framework, the non-local potentials defined as V^𝐱,𝐱′n​l​ΨT​(𝐱′)ΨT​(𝐱)\hat{V}^{nl}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}\cfrac{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}{{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right)} is nothing but ⟨x|V^li,I​P^li,I|xm⟩​⟨xm|ΨT⟩⟨x|ΨT⟩\braket{x|\hat{V}_{l}^{i,I}\hat{P}_{l}^{i,I}|x_{m}}\cfrac{\braket{x_{m}|\Psi_{\text{T}}}}{\braket{x|\Psi_{\text{T}}}} for nucleus II and electron ii. Therefore, within the discretized summation implementation, one needs to consider only the non-diagonal hoppings 𝐱→𝐱′\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}^{\prime} satisfying |𝐫i′−𝐑I|=|𝐫i−𝐑I||\mathbf{r}^{\prime}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|=|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|. Indeed, one should considers only NV⋅Na⋅NeN_{V}\cdot N_{a}\cdot N_{e} non-diagonal matrix elements at maximum for the non-local PP term, even if, in practice, we can consider only a few neighboring atoms II to the target electron index ii since the potential decays exponentially, resulting in reducing the mesh size that should be considered to ∼NV⋅Ne\sim N_{V}\cdot N_{e}.

With the semi-local ECPs, the fixed-node Hamiltonian (Eq. 17) corresponds to the T-move approximation of the standard DMC framework [16]. If one replaces 𝒱𝐱,𝐱′nl​ΨT​(𝐱′)/ΨT​(𝐱){{\mathcal{V}^{\rm nl}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}}{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}/{\Psi_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right) with 𝒱𝐱,𝐱′nl​DT​(𝐱′)/DT​(𝐱){{\mathcal{V}^{\rm nl}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}}{D_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\right)}/{D_{\text{T}}}\left(\mathbf{x}\right), where DTD_{\text{T}} represents the determinant part of the trial wave function ΨT\Psi_{\text{T}}, the resultant fixed-node Hamiltonian corresponds to T-move with determinant locality approximation (DTM) in the standard DMC framework [97]. jQMC implements the two fixed-node Hamiltonians for calculations with ECPs.

V Derivatives of total energy

The total-energy derivatives with respect to the variational parameters are a key component in order to optimize the many-body wave function. Similarly, those with respect to atomic coordinates (i.e., atomic forces) are essential for tasks such as geometry optimization, phonon dispersion calculations, and for making machine-learning interatomic potentials. Algorithmic Differentiation or Automatic Differentiation (AD) offers a powerful solution to this problem by systematically applying the chain rule [79]. AD comes in two primary forms: forward-mode AD (FAD), which propagates derivatives from the inputs to the outputs, and adjoint-mode AD (AAD), which starts from the outputs to the inputs. They correspond to Jacobian-Vector products (JVPs) and Vector-Jacobian products (VJPs) in the JAX terminology [11], respectively. When the number of input parameters significantly exceeds the number of outputs, AAD is more efficient, as it enables the evaluation of all gradients in a computational time comparable to that of a single function evaluation (e.g., the energy or wave function). This computational advantage makes AAD particularly well-suited for QMC simulations involving wave functions with many variational parameters. AAD was first introduced in the QMC context for atomic force calculations in Ref. 79. Our implementation, jQMC, leverages AAD provided by JAX (e.g. grad) to efficiently compute derivatives of the local energy and the logarithm of the wave function.

V.1 Derivatives with respect to variational parameters (MCMC)

The energy derivative with respect to a variational parameter αk{\alpha_{k}} is represented as a generalized force:

fk=−∂E⁡(𝜶)∂αk=−∂∂αk​⟨Ψ𝜶|ℋ^|Ψ𝜶⟩⟨Ψ𝜶|Ψ𝜶⟩.{f_{k}}=-\frac{{\partial E\left(\bm{\alpha}\right)}}{{\partial{\alpha_{k}}}}=-\frac{\partial}{{\partial{\alpha_{k}}}}\frac{{\braket{{\Psi^{\bm{\alpha}}}|\hat{\mathcal{H}}|{\Psi^{\bm{\alpha}}}}}}{{\braket{{\Psi^{\bm{\alpha}}}|{\Psi^{\bm{\alpha}}}}}}. (93)

In MCMC, the derivative can be evaluated using MM configurations of electron coordinates [8]:

fk=−2​∑𝐱eL​(𝐱)​(Ok​(𝐱)−O¯k)​|Ψ𝜶​(𝐱)|2∑𝐱|Ψ𝜶​(𝐱)|2≈−2​∑i=1Mwi​eL​(𝐱i)​(Ok​(𝐱i)−O¯k)∑i=1Mwi,\begin{split}{f_{k}}&=-2\,\cfrac{\sum_{\mathbf{x}}e_{L}(\mathbf{x})\left(O_{k}(\mathbf{x})-\bar{O}_{k}\right)|\Psi^{\bm{\alpha}}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}}{\sum_{\mathbf{x}}|\Psi^{\bm{\alpha}}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}}\\ &\approx-2\,\cfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}\,e_{L}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\left(O_{k}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-\bar{O}_{k}\right)}{\sum_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}},\end{split} (94)

where eL​(𝐱){e_{L}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}}}\right)} is the local energy, Ok​(𝐱){O_{k}}\left({\mathbf{x}}\right) is the logarithmic derivative of the WF, i.e., Ok​(𝐱)=∂∂αk​ln⁡Ψ𝜶​(𝐱){O_{k}}\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)=\cfrac{\partial}{{\partial{\alpha_{k}}}}\ln{\Psi^{\bm{\alpha}}}\left({\mathbf{x}}\right)), and O¯k{{\bar{O}}_{k}} is its average over MM samples, i.e., O¯k=∑i=1Mwi​Ok​(𝐱i)/∑i=1Mwi{{\bar{O}}_{k}}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}{O_{k}}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right)/\sum\limits_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}. In jQMC, the logarithmic derivative Ok​(𝐱){O_{k}}\left({\mathbf{x}}\right) is computed via JAX’s automatic differentiation (grad) functionality. In jQMC, the derivatives with respect to the wave function parameters are implemented only for MCMC at present; in the future, they will be implemented also for LRDMC.

V.2 Derivatives with respect to nuclear coordinates: Atomic forces (MCMC)

jQMC employs the differential form of atomic force calculations with the space-warp coordinate transformation (SWCT) technique to reduce the statistical error [91]:

𝐅I=−⟨dd​𝐑I​eL⟩+2​[⟨eL⟩​⟨dd​𝐑I​log⁡(𝒥12​Ψ)⟩−⟨eL​dd​𝐑I​log⁡(𝒥12​Ψ)⟩]{{\mathbf{F}}_{I}}=-\left\langle{\frac{d}{{d{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}}}{e_{L}}}\right\rangle+2\left[{\left\langle{{e_{L}}}\right\rangle\left\langle{\frac{d}{{d{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}}}\log\left({{{\mathcal{J}}^{\frac{1}{2}}}\Psi}\right)}\right\rangle-\left\langle{{e_{L}}\,\frac{d}{{d{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}}}\log\left({{{\mathcal{J}}^{\frac{1}{2}}}\Psi}\right)}\right\rangle}\right] (95)

where 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} is the Jacobian of the SWCT. The SWCT is used to follow the displacement of charges around the nucleus,

𝐫¯i=𝐫i+d​𝐑I​ωI​(𝐫i),{{\mathbf{\bar{r}}}_{i}}={{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}+d{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}{\omega_{I}}\left({{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}\right), (96)
ωI​(𝐫)=κ⁡(|𝐫−𝐑I|)∑J=1Naκ⁡(|𝐫−𝐑J|),{\omega_{I}}\left({\mathbf{r}}\right)=\frac{{\kappa\left({\left|{{\mathbf{r}}-{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}}\right|}\right)}}{{\sum\nolimits_{{J}=1}^{N_{\text{a}}}{\kappa\left({\left|{{\mathbf{r}}-{{\mathbf{R}}_{J}}}\right|}\right)}}}, (97)

where κ⁡(r){\kappa\left(r\right)} is a function that decays sufficiently fast for large rr. The original[91] choice, κ⁡(r)=1/r4\kappa\left(r\right)=1/{r^{4}}, is adopted in jQMC. The parameter derivatives are computed with the partial derivatives of the local energy and those of the logarithm of the wavefunction [79]:

𝐅IVMC=−d​Ed​𝐑I=\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{I}^{\rm VMC}=-\frac{dE}{d\mathbf{R}_{I}}= −\displaystyle- ⟨∂EL∂𝐑I+∑iω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i)​∂EL∂𝐫i⟩\displaystyle\braket{\frac{\partial E_{\rm L}}{\partial\mathbf{R}_{I}}+\sum\limits_{i}{{\omega}\left({\mathbf{R}}_{I},{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}\right)\frac{\partial E_{\rm L}}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}}}} (98)
−\displaystyle- 2​⟨(EL−E)​(∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐑I+∑i[ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i)​∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐫i+12​∂ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i)∂𝐫i])⟩.\displaystyle 2\braket{(E_{\rm L}-E)\left(\frac{\partial\log\Psi}{\partial\mathbf{R}_{I}}+\sum\limits_{i}{\left[{{\omega}\left({\mathbf{R}}_{I},{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}\right)\frac{\partial\log\Psi}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial{\omega}\left({{{\mathbf{R}}_{I},{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}\right)}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}}}\right]}\right)}.

Here, 6NeN_{e} + 6NaN_{\rm a} components have to be evaluated, i.e., ⟨∂EL∂𝐫i⟩\left\langle{\cfrac{\partial{E_{L}}}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}}}\right\rangle, ⟨∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐫i⟩\left\langle{\cfrac{\partial\log\Psi}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}}}\right\rangle, ⟨∂EL∂𝐑I⟩\left\langle{\cfrac{\partial{E_{L}}}{{\partial{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}}}}\right\rangle, ⟨∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐑I⟩\left\langle{\cfrac{\partial\log\Psi}{{\partial{{\mathbf{R}}_{I}}}}}\right\rangle [79]. The dimensions of ∂EL∂𝐑I\cfrac{\partial E_{\rm L}}{\partial\mathbf{R}_{I}}, ∂EL∂𝐫i\cfrac{\partial E_{\rm L}}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}}, ∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐑I\cfrac{\partial\log\Psi}{\partial\mathbf{R}_{I}}, ∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐫i\cfrac{\partial\log\Psi}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}}, and ∂ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i)∂𝐫i\cfrac{\partial{\omega}\left({{{\mathbf{R}}_{I},{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}\right)}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}} are (Na,3)(N_{a},3), (Ne,3)(N_{e},3), (Na,3)(N_{a},3), (Ne,3)(N_{e},3), and (Na,Ne,3)(N_{a},N_{e},3), respectively. ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i){\omega}\left({\mathbf{R}}_{I},{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}}}\right) is always a scalar value. One can define the following matrices to compute the force components with a given electronic configuration 𝐱\mathbf{x}:

{∂ER≡∂EL∂𝐑Id​i​m.=(Na,3),∂Er,↑≡∂EL∂𝐫i↑d​i​m.=(Ne↑,3),∂Er,↓≡∂EL∂𝐫i↓d​i​m.=(Ne↓,3),∂ΨR≡∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐑Id​i​m.=(Na,3),∂Ψr,↑≡∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐫i↑d​i​m.=(Ne↑,3),∂Ψr,↓≡∂log⁡Ψ∂𝐫i↓d​i​m.=(Ne↓,3),∂Ωr,↑≡∑i∂ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i↑)∂𝐫i↑d​i​m.=(Na,3),∂Ωr,↓≡∑i∂ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i↓)∂𝐫i↓d​i​m.=(Na,3),Ω↑≡ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i↑)d​i​m.=(Na,Ne↑).Ω↓≡ω⁡(𝐑I,𝐫i↓)d​i​m.=(Na,Ne↓).\begin{cases}\partial E^{R}\equiv\cfrac{\partial E_{\rm L}}{\partial\mathbf{R}_{I}}&dim.=(N_{a},3),\\ \partial E^{r,\uparrow}\equiv\cfrac{\partial E_{\rm L}}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\uparrow}}}}&dim.=(N_{e}^{\uparrow},3),\\ \partial E^{r,\downarrow}\equiv\cfrac{\partial E_{\rm L}}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\downarrow}}}}&dim.=(N_{e}^{\downarrow},3),\\ \partial\Psi^{R}\equiv\cfrac{\partial\log\Psi}{\partial\mathbf{R}_{I}}&dim.=(N_{a},3),\\ \partial\Psi^{r,\uparrow}\equiv\cfrac{\partial\log\Psi}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\uparrow}}}}&dim.=(N_{e}^{\uparrow},3),\\ \partial\Psi^{r,\downarrow}\equiv\cfrac{\partial\log\Psi}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\downarrow}}}}&dim.=(N_{e}^{\downarrow},3),\\ \partial\Omega^{r,\uparrow}\equiv\sum_{i}\cfrac{\partial{\omega}\left({{{\mathbf{R}}_{I},{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\uparrow}}}\right)}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\uparrow}}}}&dim.=(N_{a},3),\\ \partial\Omega^{r,\downarrow}\equiv\sum_{i}\cfrac{\partial{\omega}\left({{{\mathbf{R}}_{I},{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\downarrow}}}\right)}{{\partial{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\downarrow}}}}&dim.=(N_{a},3),\\ \Omega^{\uparrow}\equiv{\omega}\left({\mathbf{R}}_{I},{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\uparrow}}}\right)&dim.=(N_{a},N_{e}^{\uparrow}).\\ \Omega^{\downarrow}\equiv{\omega}\left({\mathbf{R}}_{I},{{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}^{\downarrow}}}\right)&dim.=(N_{a},N_{e}^{\downarrow}).\\ \end{cases} (99)

Once the objects in Eq. 99 are evaluated and stored, the (Na,3)(N_{\rm a},3) force matrix FVMC{F}^{\rm VMC} can be obtained via matrix-matrix operations, according to the following contributions:

FVMC=FHF+FPulay,{F}^{\rm VMC}={F}^{\rm HF}+{F}^{\rm Pulay}, (100)

where the Hellmann–Feynman (HF) term is

FHF=−⟨∂ER+Ω↑​∂Er,↑+Ω↓​∂Er,↓⟩,{F}^{\rm HF}=-\braket{\partial E^{R}+\Omega^{\uparrow}\partial E^{r,\uparrow}+\Omega^{\downarrow}\partial E^{r,\downarrow}}, (101)

and the Pulay contribution reads

FPulay\displaystyle{F}^{\rm Pulay} =\displaystyle= −2​⟨(EL−E)​(∂ΨR+Ω↑​∂Ψr,↑+Ω↓​∂Ψr,↓+12​(∂Ωr,↑+∂Ωr,↓))⟩.\displaystyle-2\braket{(E_{\rm L}-E)(\partial\Psi^{R}+\Omega^{\uparrow}\partial\Psi^{r,\uparrow}+\Omega^{\downarrow}\partial\Psi^{r,\downarrow}+\cfrac{1}{2}(\partial\Omega^{r,\uparrow}+\partial\Omega^{r,\downarrow}))}. (102)

We validated the force implementation through the PES calculation of the Hydrogen and Nitrogen dimer. To test the implementation, we verified that the the following conditions are satisfied: (a) The derivative of the PES with respect to the bond distance should be consistent with the computed atomic forces as long as all the parameters are variationally optimized, and (b), with the SWCT, the atomic forces acting on the left and right atoms of a dimer should have exactly the same absolute values [49].

V.3 Derivatives with respect to nuclear coordinates: Atomic forces (LRDMC)

In LRDMC, the atomic force computation differs from the MCMC case (Sec. V.2) in three respects: (i) the SWCT is not recommended because it leads to a bias, (ii) the Reynolds approximation [68] is introduced to replace the inaccessible derivative ∂Ψ0/∂𝐑I\partial\Psi_{0}/\partial\mathbf{R}_{I} with the available ∂ΨT/∂𝐑I\partial\Psi_{T}/\partial\mathbf{R}_{I}, and (iii) the Pathak-Wagner [58] regularization is applied to suppress the divergence of the local energy derivative near the nodal surface.

Since the SWCT is typically not used in LRDMC, all Ω\Omega terms vanish (ωI=0\omega_{I}=0), and the force expression simplifies considerably. Using the same shorthand notation defined in Sec. V.2, the force on atom II sampled from the mixed distribution ΨT​Ψ0\Psi_{\rm T}\Psi_{0} reads:

FImixed=FmixedHF+FmixedPulay,{F}_{I}^{\rm mixed}={F}^{\rm HF}_{\rm mixed}+{F}^{\rm Pulay}_{\rm mixed}, (103)

where

FmixedHF=−⟨∂ER⟩ΨT​Ψ0,{F}^{\rm HF}_{\rm mixed}=-\braket{\partial E^{R}}_{\Psi_{\rm T}\Psi_{0}}, (104)
FmixedPulay=−2​⟨(EL−E)​∂ΨR⟩ΨT​Ψ0.{F}^{\rm Pulay}_{\rm mixed}=-2\braket{(E_{\rm L}-E)\,\partial\Psi^{R}}_{\Psi_{\rm T}\Psi_{0}}. (105)

Here, ⟨⋅⟩ΨT​Ψ0\braket{\cdot}_{\Psi_{\rm T}\Psi_{0}} denotes the average over the mixed distribution sampled by the LRDMC walker population, in contrast to the MCMC average over ΨT2\Psi_{\rm T}^{2}. The mixed estimator FImixed{F}_{I}^{\rm mixed} is biased because the sampling distribution ΨT​Ψ0\Psi_{\rm T}\Psi_{0} differs from the pure distribution Ψ02\Psi_{0}^{2}. This approximation becomes exact when ΨT=Ψ0\Psi_{\rm T}=\Psi_{0}.

Near the nodal surface of ΨT\Psi_{\rm T}, the local energy and its derivatives can diverge, leading to large statistical fluctuations in the force estimator. To mitigate this issue, we employ the Pathak–Wagner regularization [58]. According to the reweighting method, the bracket ⟨O⟩\braket{O} is evaluated using the regularized estimator with a function Rη​(𝐱)R_{\eta}(\mathbf{x}):

O¯=⟨O⁡(𝐱)​Rη​(𝐱)⟩.\bar{O}=\braket{O(\mathbf{x})\,R_{\eta}(\mathbf{x})}. (106)

Here,

Rη​(𝐱)={7​|𝜻/η|6−15​|𝜻/η|4+9​|𝜻/η|2,|𝜻/η|≤1,1,|𝜻/η|>1,R_{\eta}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}7\bigl|\bm{\zeta}/\eta\bigr|^{6}-15\bigl|\bm{\zeta}/\eta\bigr|^{4}+9\bigl|\bm{\zeta}/\eta\bigr|^{2},&\bigl|\bm{\zeta}/\eta\bigr|\leq 1,\\ 1,&\bigl|\bm{\zeta}/\eta\bigr|>1,\end{cases} (107)

with

𝜻=Ψ(𝐱)∇Ψ(𝐱)|∇Ψ​(𝐱)|2.\bm{\zeta}=\cfrac{\Psi(\mathbf{x})\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{x})}{|\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}}. (108)

Here, ∇\nabla denotes the many-body gradient, collecting all particle-coordinate derivatives into a single vector. Defining

Qi,k≡∂∂ri,k​Ψ​(𝐱),Q_{i,k}\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{i,k}}\Psi(\mathbf{x}), (109)

one may regard 𝐐\mathbf{Q} as an (Ne,3)(N_{e},3) matrix. Then,

|∇Ψ​(𝐱)|2=‖𝐐‖F2,|\nabla\Psi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}=\|\mathbf{Q}\|_{F}^{2}, (110)

and

|𝜻/η|=|Ψ⁡(𝐱)|η​‖𝐐‖F,\bigl|\bm{\zeta}/\eta\bigr|=\frac{|\Psi(\mathbf{x})|}{\eta\,\|\mathbf{Q}\|_{F}}, (111)

where ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{F} denotes the Frobenius norm. The quantity 𝜻\bm{\zeta} represents the normal distance between 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the nearest nodal point of Ψ\Psi, while η\eta controls the distance from the nodal surface within which the regularization is applied.

Each expectation values entering the total force are regularized as follows:

FmixedHF=−⟨∂ER⋅Rη​(𝐱)⟩ΨT​Ψ0,{F}^{\rm HF}_{\rm mixed}=-\braket{\partial E^{R}\cdot R_{\eta}(\mathbf{x})}_{\Psi_{\rm T}\Psi_{0}}, (112)
FmixedPulay=−2​⟨(EL−E)​∂ΨR⋅Rη​(𝐱)⟩ΨT​Ψ0,{F}^{\rm Pulay}_{\rm mixed}=-2\braket{(E_{\rm L}-E)\,\partial\Psi^{R}\cdot R_{\eta}(\mathbf{x})}_{\Psi_{\rm T}\Psi_{0}}, (113)

where Rη​(𝐱)R_{\eta}(\mathbf{x}) is the regularization function defined in Eq. (107), which smoothly suppresses contributions from walkers within a distance η\eta of the nodal surface.

VI Optimization of WFs

Optimizing the variational parameters of the many-body wave function is the most challenging task in ab initio QMC calculations. Since the QMC energy (and sometimes the variance) is evaluated stochastically and is strongly nonlinear in the variational parameters, a straightforward optimization method such as gradient descent does not work and is extremely inefficient. The wave-function optimization in the context of ab initio QMC has been studied for a long time. Stochastic Reconfiguration (SR)  [81] developed by Sorella, the Linear method (LM)  [90] developed by Umrigar et al., and their variants  [90, 88, 80] are the most widely adopted optimization methods in the QMC community. jQMC implements both of them.
