In both SR and LR, the metric for the parameter space (𝓢{\bm{\mathcal{S}}}), which measures the distance of the underlying normalized wavefunction [36], plays a central role. The normalized wavefunction at the given variational parameters α\alpha is defined as

|Ψ~α⟩=|Ψα⟩/⟨Ψα|Ψα⟩,\ket{\tilde{\Psi}^{\alpha}}=\ket{\Psi^{\alpha}}/\sqrt{\braket{\Psi^{\alpha}|\Psi^{\alpha}}}, (114)

while its derivatives with respect to the variational parameters define a semi-orthogonal basis set:

|Ψ~kα⟩=∂∂αk|Ψ~α⟩=(O^k−O¯k)|Ψ~α⟩,k=1,…,P,\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\alpha_{k}}\ket{\tilde{\Psi}^{\alpha}}=(\hat{O}_{k}-\bar{O}_{k})\ket{\tilde{\Psi}^{\alpha}},\qquad k=1,\ldots,P, (115)

where PP is the total number of variational parameters, O^k\hat{O}_{k} is the logarithmic derivative operator, whose sample-wise representation, introduced in Sec. V.1, is Ok​(𝐱)=∂log⁡Ψα​(𝐱)/∂αkO_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\partial\log\Psi^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x})/\partial\alpha_{k}, and O¯k=⟨Ψ~α|O^k|Ψ~α⟩\bar{O}_{k}=\braket{\tilde{\Psi}^{\alpha}|\hat{O}_{k}|\tilde{\Psi}^{\alpha}} is its expectation value. Then, the metric for the parameter space (𝓢{\bm{\mathcal{S}}}), which is based on the overlap matrix between the semi-orthogonal basis components, is computed as:

𝒮k,k′=⟨Ψ~kα|Ψ~k′α⟩≡⟨Ψ~α|(O^k−O¯k)​(O^k′−O¯k′)|Ψ~α⟩=⟨Ψα|(O^k−O¯k)​(O^k′−O¯k′)|Ψα⟩⟨Ψα|Ψα⟩.\mathcal{S}_{k,k^{\prime}}=\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k^{\prime}}^{\alpha}}\equiv\braket{\tilde{\Psi}^{\alpha}|(\hat{O}_{k}-\bar{O}_{k})(\hat{O}_{k^{\prime}}-\bar{O}_{k^{\prime}})|\tilde{\Psi}^{\alpha}}=\frac{\braket{{\Psi}^{\alpha}|(\hat{O}_{k}-\bar{O}_{k})(\hat{O}_{k^{\prime}}-\bar{O}_{k^{\prime}})|{\Psi}^{\alpha}}}{\braket{{\Psi}^{\alpha}|{\Psi}^{\alpha}}}. (116)

VI.1 Stochastic Reconfiguration (a.k.a. natural gradient optimization)

SR is a nonlinear optimization method for many-body wave functions developed by Sorella[81]. It uses a positive-definite preconditioning matrix 𝓢{\bm{\mathcal{S}}} which represents the metric of the parameter space (Eq. 116), and the generalized force vector 𝐟\mathbf{f} (Eq. 93), such that during an optimization step the WF parameters are updated as follows:

αk→αk+Δ⋅(𝓢−1​𝐟)k.{\alpha_{k}}\to{\alpha_{k}}+\Delta\cdot{\left({{{\bm{\mathcal{S}}}^{-1}}{\mathbf{f}}}\right)_{k}}. (117)

The matrix 𝓢{\bm{\mathcal{S}}} is stochastically evaluated using MM samples 𝐱={𝐱1,𝐱2,…​𝐱M}{\mathbf{x}}=\left\{{{{\mathbf{x}}_{1}},{{\mathbf{x}}_{2}},\ldots{{\mathbf{x}}_{M}}}\right\} (for the simple MCMC) with weights w={w1,w2,…​wM}{w}=\left\{w_{1},w_{2},\ldots w_{M}\right\} (for the weighted MCMC):

𝒮k,k′=∑i=1Mwi​(Ok​(𝐱i)−O¯k)​(Ok′​(𝐱i)−O¯k′)∑i=1Mwi,{{\mathcal{S}}_{k,k^{\prime}}}=\frac{{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}{\left({{O_{k}}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right)-{{\bar{O}}_{k}}}\right)\left({{O_{k^{\prime}}}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right)-{{\bar{O}}_{k^{\prime}}}}\right)}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}}, (118)

where Ok​(𝐱i)=∂∂αk​log⁡Ψα​(𝐱i){O_{k}}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right)=\cfrac{\partial}{{\partial{\alpha_{k}}}}{\log\Psi^{\alpha}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right)}, O¯k=∑i=1Mwi​Ok​(𝐱i)/∑i=1Mwi{{\bar{O}}_{k}}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{M}{w_{i}{O_{k}}\left({{{\mathbf{x}}_{i}}}\right)}/\sum\limits_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}, and 𝐟\mathbf{f} is computed as in Eq. 94 of Sec. V.1. We notice that the natural gradient method [4] developed by Amari et al. in a different context and used for machine learning in recent years has a direct correspondence with the SR.

The native SR method often suffers from numerical instabilities because the statistical noise makes the matrix 𝓢{\bm{\mathcal{S}}} ill-conditioned [80]. jQMC mitigates the problem by the following numerical technique. First, to simplify the computation [67] and to stabilize the solution, jQMC introduces the quantities

Xk,i≡Xk​(xi)=wi​(Ok​(xi)−O¯k)∑i=1Mwi,X_{k,i}\equiv X_{k}(x_{i})=\frac{\sqrt{w_{i}}(O_{k}(x_{i})-\bar{O}_{k})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}}}, (119)

and

ei≡e⁡(xi)=−2​wi​(eL​(xi)−e¯L)∑i=1Mwi,e_{i}\equiv e(x_{i})=\frac{-2\sqrt{w_{i}}({e_{L}}(x_{i})-{\bar{e}_{L}})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{M}w_{i}}}, (120)

which give 𝓢=X​XT\bm{\mathcal{S}}=XX^{T} and 𝐟=X​e\mathbf{f}=Xe. To make 𝓢\bm{\mathcal{S}} scale-invariant [8], XX is rescaled row-wise by the inverse square root of the diagonal of 𝓢\bm{\mathcal{S}}:

Xk,i←Xk,i/𝒮k,k.X_{k,i}\leftarrow X_{k,i}/\sqrt{\mathcal{S}_{k,k}}. (121)

Notice that ee does not need to be rescaled separately, since the rescaling of 𝐟\mathbf{f} is considered via 𝐟=X​e\mathbf{f}=Xe. In this normalized basis, the regularized SR update reads

δ​θ=τ​(X​XT+εSR​IP)−1​X​e,\delta\theta=\tau(XX^{T}+\varepsilon_{\rm SR}I_{P})^{-1}Xe, (122)

where PP is the total number of variational parameters. After solving for δ​θ\delta\theta in the normalized basis, the natural-gradient direction is rescaled back via δ​θk←δ​θk/𝒮k,k\delta\theta_{k}\leftarrow\delta\theta_{k}/\sqrt{\mathcal{S}_{k,k}}.

The above reformulation also enables the use of the well-known push-through identity technique [28, 60], namely (A​B+λ​I)−1​A=A​(B​A+λ​I)−1(AB+\lambda I)^{-1}A=A(BA+\lambda I)^{-1}:

δ​θ=τ​X​(XT​X+εSR​IM)−1​e,\delta\theta=\tau X(X^{T}X+\varepsilon_{\rm SR}I_{M})^{-1}e, (123)

which is more efficient when the number of samples MM is smaller than the number of parameters PP.

Either with or without the push-through identity technique, jQMC does not compute the inverse of the matrix X​XTXX^{T} or XT​XX^{T}X. Instead, it solves the inversion problem using the conjugate gradient (CG) method. Let each MPI rank hold a local block X(d)∈ℝP×MdX^{(d)}\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times M_{d}}, where PP is the number of variational parameters and MdM_{d} is the number of MCMC samples held by rank dd. The global XX is then X=[X(1),X(2),…,X(D)]∈ℝP×M,M=∑d=1DMd.X=\bigl[\,X^{(1)},\,X^{(2)},\,\dots,\,X^{(D)}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times M},\quad M=\sum_{d=1}^{D}M_{d}. In the CG mode, jQMC never assembles 𝓢≡X​XT\bm{\mathcal{S}}\equiv XX^{T} ∈ℝP×P\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times P} or XT​XX^{T}X ∈ℝM×M\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}; it only stores the distributed blocks X(d)X^{(d)} and auxiliary vectors. More specifically, jQMC implements a matrix-free CG method to solve (𝓢+εSR​IP)​θ=𝐟\bigl(\bm{\mathcal{S}}+\varepsilon_{\rm SR}I_{P}\bigr)\,\theta=\mathbf{f} (or its dual form), where each rank dd independently computes only its local matrix-vector contributions. Indeed, before starting the CG iterations, the right-hand side is constructed as 𝐟=∑d=1DX(d)​e(d)\mathbf{f}=\sum_{d=1}^{D}X^{(d)}e^{(d)}, where all ranks first compute their local contributions (X(d)​e(d)X^{(d)}e^{(d)}), summed them up using a global all-reduce. Then, during the CG iterations, each rank repeatedly computes its local contribution, v↦X(d)​(X(d)​T​v),v\mapsto X^{(d)}\left(X^{(d)T}v\right), and a global all-reduce is then used to obtain v↦∑d=1DX(d)​(X(d)​T​v)+εSR​v.v\mapsto\sum_{d=1}^{D}X^{(d)}\left(X^{(d)T}v\right)+\varepsilon_{\rm SR}v. This naturally distributes both memory and compute workloads among CPUs or GPUs, yielding excellent weak-scaling behavior without storing the full SR matrix, as demonstrated in Sec. XII.

In practice, during an optimization, jQMC monitors the variational energy (EE) and the maximum value of the signal to noise ratio among all the force components:

signal-to-noise ratio≡maxk⁡(|fkσfk|)\verb| signal-to-noise ratio|\equiv\max_{k}\left({\left|{\frac{{{f_{k}}}}{{{\sigma_{{f_{k}}}}}}}\right|}\right) (124)

where σfk{\sigma_{{f_{k}}}} represents the estimated error bar of the force fk{f_{k}}. This value is used in jQMC as one of the convergence criteria of the WF optimization.

VI.2 The Linear method and its variants

The LM starts from the linear expansion of the normalized variational wave function with respect to the variational parameters 𝜶\bm{\alpha}:

|Ψ~0α+δ​𝜶⟩=|Ψ~0α⟩+∑k=1pδ​αk​|Ψ~kα⟩≡∑k=0pzk​|Ψ~kα⟩,\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha+\delta\bm{\alpha}}}=\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha}}+\sum_{k=1}^{p}\delta\alpha_{k}\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}}\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p}z_{k}\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}}, (125)

where z0=1z_{0}=1 and zk=δ​αkz_{k}=\delta\alpha_{k} for k≥1k\geq 1. Here, |Ψ~0,α⟩≡|Ψ~α⟩\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0,\alpha}}\equiv\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{\alpha}} is the normalized wavefunction defined in Eq. 114, and |Ψ~k,α⟩\ket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k,\alpha}} is the semi-orthogonal basis defined in Eq. 115. By construction, this basis satisfies ⟨Ψ~0α|Ψ~kα⟩=0\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}}=0 for all k≥1k\geq 1. Using this expansion, the variational energy is written as

Eα+δ​𝜶=⟨Ψ~0α+δ​𝜶|H^|Ψ~0α+δ​𝜶⟩⟨Ψ~0α+δ​𝜶|Ψ~0α+δ​𝜶⟩=∑k,k′=0pzk​zk′​⟨Ψ~kα|H^|Ψ~k′α⟩∑k,k′=0pzk​zk′​⟨Ψ~kα|Ψ~k′α⟩.E_{\alpha+\delta\bm{\alpha}}=\frac{\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha+\delta\bm{\alpha}}|\hat{H}|\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha+\delta\bm{\alpha}}}}{\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha+\delta\bm{\alpha}}|\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha+\delta\bm{\alpha}}}}=\frac{\sum_{k,k^{\prime}=0}^{p}z_{k}z_{k^{\prime}}\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}|\hat{H}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k^{\prime}}^{\alpha}}}{\sum_{k,k^{\prime}=0}^{p}z_{k}z_{k^{\prime}}\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k^{\prime}}^{\alpha}}}. (126)

Stationarity with respect to zlz_{l} leads to the generalized eigenvalue problem

𝐇𝐳=E​𝓢​𝐳,\mathbf{H}\mathbf{z}=E\bm{\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{z}, (127)

with

Hk,k′=⟨Ψ~kα|H^|Ψ~k′α⟩,𝒮k,k′=⟨Ψ~kα|Ψ~k′α⟩.H_{k,k^{\prime}}=\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}|\hat{H}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k^{\prime}}^{\alpha}},\qquad\mathcal{S}_{k,k^{\prime}}=\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k^{\prime}}^{\alpha}}. (128)

The matrix elements can be evaluated efficiently by Monte Carlo sampling over π⁡(𝐱)∝|Ψα​(𝐱)|2\pi(\mathbf{x})\propto|\Psi^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}. In particular,

⟨Ψ~kα|H^|Ψ~k′α⟩=⟨(Ok​(𝐱)−O¯k)​Wk′​(𝐱)⟩π⁡(𝐱),\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}|\hat{H}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k^{\prime}}^{\alpha}}=\left\langle(O_{k}(\mathbf{x})-\bar{O}_{k})\,W_{k^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle_{\pi(\mathbf{x})}, (129)

where

Wk​(𝐱)=⟨x|H^​(O^k−O¯k)|Ψα⟩⟨x|Ψα⟩.W_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\braket{x|\hat{H}(\hat{O}_{k}-\bar{O}_{k})|\Psi^{\alpha}}}{\braket{x|\Psi^{\alpha}}}. (130)

This quantity is related to the derivatives of the local energy:

∂EL​(𝐱)∂αk=⟨x|H^​(O^k−O¯k)|Ψ~0,α⟩⟨x|Ψ~0,α⟩−EL​(𝐱)​(Ok​(𝐱)−O¯k),\frac{\partial E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial\alpha_{k}}=\frac{\braket{x|\hat{H}(\hat{O}_{k}-\bar{O}_{k})|\tilde{\Psi}_{0,\alpha}}}{\braket{x|\tilde{\Psi}_{0,\alpha}}}-E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})(O_{k}(\mathbf{x})-\bar{O}_{k}), (131)

so that

Wk​(𝐱)=∂EL​(𝐱)∂αk+EL​(𝐱)​(Ok​(𝐱)−O¯k).W_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\partial E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial\alpha_{k}}+E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})(O_{k}(\mathbf{x})-\bar{O}_{k}). (132)

We notice that if the local energy is real, then ⟨∂EL​(𝐱)/∂αk⟩=0\left\langle\partial E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})/\partial\alpha_{k}\right\rangle=0 (see Ref. 82). Substituting Eq. (132) into Eq. (129), the LM Hamiltonian matrix is naturally decomposed as 𝐇=𝐊+𝐁\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{B}, with

Kk,k′\displaystyle K_{k,k^{\prime}} =⟨δ​Ok​(𝐱)​δ​Ok′​(𝐱)​EL​(𝐱)⟩π⁡(𝐱),\displaystyle=\langle\,\delta O_{k}(\mathbf{x})\,\delta O_{k^{\prime}}(\mathbf{x})\,E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})\,\rangle_{\pi(\mathbf{x})}, (133)
Bk,k′\displaystyle B_{k,k^{\prime}} =⟨δ​Ok​(𝐱)​∂EL​(𝐱)∂αk′⟩π⁡(𝐱),\displaystyle=\langle\,\delta O_{k}(\mathbf{x})\,\frac{\partial E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial\alpha_{k^{\prime}}}\,\rangle_{\pi(\mathbf{x})}, (134)

where δ​Ok​(𝐱)=Ok​(𝐱)−O¯k\delta O_{k}(\mathbf{x})=O_{k}(\mathbf{x})-\bar{O}_{k}. The KK matrix is symmetric in kk and k′k^{\prime}, whereas BB inherits the asymmetry of the WW derivation. Since the exact 𝐇\mathbf{H} is hermitian (symmetric for the real wave functions considered in this study), 𝐊+𝐁\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{B} is symmetrized post-hoc as 𝐇←(𝐇+𝐇T)/2\mathbf{H}\leftarrow(\mathbf{H}+\mathbf{H}^{T})/2 in jQMC to avoid the numerical instaibility.

We note that the elements of the LM overlap (𝒮\mathcal{S}) and Hamiltonian (HH) matrices involving the zeroth basis state are given as follows. Since the derivative basis is semi-orthogonal to the current normalized wave function, we have 𝒮00=1\mathcal{S}_{00}=1 and 𝒮0​k=𝒮k​0=0(k≥1)\mathcal{S}_{0k}=\mathcal{S}_{k0}=0\quad(k\geq 1). The corresponding Hamiltonian matrix elements are H00=⟨Ψ~0α|H^|Ψ~0α⟩=Eα,H_{00}=\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha}|\hat{H}|\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha}}=E_{\alpha}, Hk​0=⟨Ψ~kα|H^|Ψ~0α⟩=⟨δ​Ok​(𝐱)​EL​(𝐱)⟩π⁡(𝐱)=−12​fkH_{k0}=\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}|\hat{H}|\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha}}=\left\langle\delta O_{k}(\mathbf{x})E_{\rm L}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle_{\pi(\mathbf{x})}=-\cfrac{1}{2}f_{k}, and H0​k=⟨Ψ~0α|H^|Ψ~kα⟩=⟨Wk​(𝐱)⟩π⁡(𝐱)=−12​fkH_{0k}=\braket{\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha}|\hat{H}|\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}}=\left\langle W_{k}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle_{\pi(\mathbf{x})}=-\cfrac{1}{2}f_{k}. where fkf_{k} (for k≥1k\geq 1) is the same as in Eq. 93.

The original LM optimizes all PP parameters simultaneously by solving the full (P+1)×(P+1)(P+1)\times(P+1) generalized eigenvalue problem [82, 90, 88]. In practice, however, this can be numerically unstable and computationally expensive when many parameters with very different scales are present. For this reason, jQMC uses two practical variants based on the SR direction gk=(𝓢−1​𝐟)kg_{k}=(\bm{\mathcal{S}}^{-1}\mathbf{f})_{k}, inspired by the TurboRVB’s implementation [80].

VI.2.1 Linear method with only the SR direction

The first practical variant addresses a key limitation of the original LM formalism, which requires solving a generalized eigenvalue problem with all PP variational parameters. This variant keeps only the SR direction and removes all individual parameter directions. In this case, the LM update is constrained to

δ​αk=γ​gk,gk=(𝓢−1​𝐟)k,\delta\alpha_{k}=\gamma g_{k},\qquad g_{k}=(\bm{\mathcal{S}}^{-1}\mathbf{f})_{k}, (135)

so that the optimization reduces to a single scalar γ\gamma. The energy becomes

Eα+δ​𝜶=H0+2​γ​H1+γ2​H21+γ2​S2,E_{\alpha+\delta\bm{\alpha}}=\frac{H_{0}+2\gamma H_{1}+\gamma^{2}H_{2}}{1+\gamma^{2}S_{2}}, (136)

with

H0=Eα,H1=−12​𝐠T​𝐟,H2=𝐠T​(𝐊+𝐁)​𝐠,S2=𝐠T​𝓢​𝐠.H_{0}=E_{\alpha},\qquad H_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{f},\qquad H_{2}=\mathbf{g}^{T}(\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{B})\,\mathbf{g},\qquad S_{2}=\mathbf{g}^{T}\bm{\mathcal{S}}\,\mathbf{g}. (137)

Minimizing E⁡(γ)E(\gamma) yields a quadratic equation,

H1​S2​γ2+(H0​S2−H2)​γ−H1=0,H_{1}S_{2}\gamma^{2}+(H_{0}S_{2}-H_{2})\gamma-H_{1}=0, (138)

whose solution is

γ=H2−H0​S2±(H2−H0​S2)2+4​H12​S22​H1​S2.\gamma=\frac{H_{2}-H_{0}S_{2}\pm\sqrt{(H_{2}-H_{0}S_{2})^{2}+4H_{1}^{2}S_{2}}}{2H_{1}S_{2}}. (139)

In jQMC, the root with the smaller absolute value is selected in order to avoid spuriously large steps. The final parameter update is simply

δ​αk=γ​gk.\delta\alpha_{k}=\gamma g_{k}. (140)

VI.2.2 Linear method with the SR collective variable and selected parameters

For a more efficient approach, we combine a single global SR collective mode, which considers the contribution of all parameters through the SR matrix 𝓢−1\bm{\mathcal{S}}^{-1}, combined with a small set of individually resolved directions corresponding to the parameters whose generalized forces have large signal-to-noise ratios. Thus, the SR direction provides a global update for all parameters, while the selected directions based on the signal-to-ratios allow the LM to assign individually optimized steps to the few chosen parameters that should be far from their local minima. Specifically, we define the SR collective state

|Ψ~SR⟩=∑k=1Pgk​|Ψ~kα⟩,gk=(𝓢−1​𝐟)k,|\tilde{\Psi}_{\mathrm{SR}}\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{P}g_{k}\,|\tilde{\Psi}_{k}^{\alpha}\rangle,\qquad g_{k}=(\bm{\mathcal{S}}^{-1}\mathbf{f})_{k}, (141)

where the sum runs over all variational parameters. The SR direction provides a well-conditioned collective mode that automatically incorporates the scale information encoded in the overlap matrix. We then diagonalize the LM in the reduced subspace

{|Ψ~0α⟩,|Ψ~SR⟩,|Ψ~k1α⟩,…,|Ψ~kmα⟩},\left\{|\tilde{\Psi}_{0}^{\alpha}\rangle,\,|\tilde{\Psi}_{\mathrm{SR}}\rangle,\,|\tilde{\Psi}_{k_{1}}^{\alpha}\rangle,\,\ldots,\,|\tilde{\Psi}_{k_{m}}^{\alpha}\rangle\right\}, (142)

where k1,…,kmk_{1},\ldots,k_{m} denote a small set of selected parameters. In jQMC, these are chosen as the parameters with the largest signal-to-noise ratio of the generalized force fkf_{k}, so that noisy directions are excluded from the explicit LM subspace. The generalized eigenvalue problem retains the same form, as in Eq. 127:

H¯​𝐯=E​𝓢¯​𝐯,\bar{H}\mathbf{v}=E\bar{\bm{\mathcal{S}}}\mathbf{v}, (143)

but now in a reduced (m+2)(m+2)-dimensional basis. The matrix elements involving the SR collective variable follow from linearity:

H¯0,SR=−12​𝐠T​𝐟,H¯SR,SR=𝐠T​(𝐊+𝐁)​𝐠,𝒮¯SR,SR=𝐠T​𝓢​𝐠,\bar{H}_{0,\mathrm{SR}}=-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}^{T}\mathbf{f},\qquad\bar{H}_{\mathrm{SR},\mathrm{SR}}=\mathbf{g}^{T}(\mathbf{K}+\mathbf{B})\,\mathbf{g},\qquad\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathrm{SR},\mathrm{SR}}=\mathbf{g}^{T}\bm{\mathcal{S}}\,\mathbf{g}, (144)

and similarly for the mixed SR-selected-parameter blocks. The final update is written as

δ​αk=vSRv0​gk+{vki/v0,k=ki∈{k1,…,km},0,otherwise.\delta\alpha_{k}=\frac{v_{\mathrm{SR}}}{v_{0}}g_{k}+\begin{cases}v_{k_{i}}/v_{0},&k=k_{i}\in\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}\},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (145)

Thus, this variant supplements the global SR direction by a few individually optimized corrections.

VI.3 Optimization of molecular orbital coefficients with constraints

In jQMC, the nodal surface of the wave function can be optimized via the determinant part, namely, the geminal matrix Λl,l′↑,↓\Lambda_{l,l^{\prime}}^{\uparrow,\downarrow} [Eq. (43)]. The most straightforward strategy is an unconstrained optimization, that is, optimizing all independent variational parameters in the geminal matrix subject only to the required symmetry. jQMC implements this simplest scheme. In addition, jQMC also implements the molecular-orbital-constrained optimization introduced in TurboRVB [33, 22, 8]. According to this scheme, one can optimize the geminal matrix Λ↑⁣↓\Lambda^{\uparrow\downarrow} expanded over the atomic orbitals (Eq. 55) by preserving a targeted rank of the matrix, chosen in input. For AGP wave functions, this approach makes it possible to introduce an effective coherence-length cutoff in the AGP matrix [8], for both insulators and metals, because the AO representation bears information on the correlation length of the geminal, through the ionic centers of the AO basis. Moreover, the AGP expanded over atomic orbitals has an equivalent natural orbital representation in its AGPn or SD form, expanded over molecular orbitals. Therefore, by constraining the rank of Λ\Lambda, the optimization can be carried out with a fixed number of molecular orbitals retained in the projection, denoted by nn (n=Ne/2n=N_{e}/2 for SD and n>Ne/2n>N_{e}/2 for AGPn), while exploiting the locality of the geminal built in the corresponding AO expansion. We describe the implementation of the fixed-rank optimization below. We notice that, following the convention stated at the beginning of Sec. II, all orbitals and the geminal matrix are taken to be real.

Below, we focus on the paired block 𝚲↑,↓\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow} of the geminal matrix; the unpaired block 𝚲↑\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow} has no spin-down index and therefore no rank constraint, and is treated separately at the end of this Subsection. To keep the formulas simple, we specialize the derivation to the spin-unpolarized SD reference, where n=Ne/2=Ne↓n=N_{e}/2=N_{e}^{\downarrow} and the nn retained MOs coincide with the occupied MOs; we therefore use the standard occupied / virtual terminology throughout the rest of the subsection instead of retained / discarded. The same formulas can be applied for AGPn (n>Ne/2n>N_{e}/2) with occupied replaced with the retained nn-dimensional MO subspace, and to the spin-polarized case via the substitutions for spin-dependent MO coefficients.

As shown in Eq. (65), the AGP pairing function (the spin-↑,↓\uparrow,\downarrow part) can be represented in the MO basis as:

F↑,↓​(𝐫,𝐫′)=∑μ=1nλμ​Φμ​(𝐫)​Φμ​(𝐫′),F^{\uparrow,\downarrow}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\sum_{\mu=1}^{n}\lambda_{\mu}\Phi_{\mu}(\mathbf{r})\Phi_{\mu}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}), (146)

where {Φμ}μ=1n\{\Phi_{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{n} are the nn occupied MOs and {λμ}\{\lambda_{\mu}\} the corresponding weights (λμ=1\lambda_{\mu}=1 for SD). Expanding the occupied MOs in the AO basis:

Φμ​(𝐫)=∑lC~l,μ​ψl​(𝐫),\Phi_{\mu}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{l}\tilde{C}_{l,\mu}\psi_{l}(\mathbf{r}), (147)

the pairing function takes the AO basis representation:

F↑,↓​(𝐫,𝐫′)=∑l,l′ψl​(𝐫)​Λl,l′↑,↓​ψl′​(𝐫′),F^{\uparrow,\downarrow}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\sum_{l,l^{\prime}}\psi_{l}(\mathbf{r})\Lambda^{\uparrow,\downarrow}_{l,l^{\prime}}\psi_{l^{\prime}}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}), (148)

with

𝚲↑,↓=𝐂~​𝝀​𝐂~T,\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow}=\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\bm{\lambda}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}, (149)

where 𝝀=diag⁡(λ1,…,λn)\bm{\lambda}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}) is the (n,n)(n,n) diagonal matrix of weights and 𝐂~\tilde{\mathbf{C}} is the (Ma​o,n)(M_{ao},n) matrix of occupied MO coefficients; thus, r​a​n​k​(𝚲↑,↓)≤nrank(\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow})\leq n. The columns of 𝐂~\tilde{\mathbf{C}} satisfy 𝐂~T​𝐒​𝐂~=In\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}=I_{n} with 𝐒\mathbf{S} being the AO overlap matrix. We notice that, in this Section, the row and column indices of the MO coefficients 𝐂~\tilde{\mathbf{C}} are flipped compared with 𝐂\mathbf{C} in Eq. 59 to follow the same notation as Ref. 8.

A linearized rank-preserving variation is obtained by changing only the quantities that appear in Eq. (149), namely 𝐂~\tilde{\mathbf{C}} and 𝝀\bm{\lambda}. Under 𝐂~→𝐂~+δ​𝐂~\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\to\tilde{\mathbf{C}}+\delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}} and 𝝀→𝝀+δ​𝝀\bm{\lambda}\to\bm{\lambda}+\delta\bm{\lambda}, the first-order variation of the geminal matrix is

(δ​𝚲↑,↓)c=δ​𝐂~​𝝀​𝐂~T+𝐂~​δ​𝝀​𝐂~T+𝐂~​𝝀​δ​𝐂~T.(\delta\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow})^{c}=\delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\,\bm{\lambda}\,\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}+\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\,\delta\bm{\lambda}\,\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}+\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\,\bm{\lambda}\,\delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}. (150)

Here, δ​𝐂~\delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}} denotes an arbitrary infinitesimal change of the occupied MO coefficients. We now introduce the AO-basis representations of the left and right projectors associated with the occupied MO subspace:

𝐑\displaystyle\mathbf{R} =(𝐒​𝐂~)​𝐂~T,\displaystyle=(\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{C}})\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}, (151)
𝐋\displaystyle\mathbf{L} =𝐑T=𝐂~​(𝐒​𝐂~)T=𝐂~​𝐂~T​𝐒,\displaystyle=\mathbf{R}^{T}=\tilde{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{C}})^{T}=\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}\mathbf{S}, (152)

where 𝐂~\tilde{\mathbf{C}} is the same MO-coefficient matrix appearing in Eq. (149), satisfying 𝐂~T​𝐒​𝐂~=In\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{C}}=I_{n}, and 𝐒\mathbf{S} is the AO overlap matrix. 𝐋\mathbf{L} acts on MO coefficient vectors from the left and is the 𝐒\mathbf{S}-orthogonal projector onto the occupied MO subspace, and thus, (𝐈−𝐋)(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L}) is the complementary projector onto the virtual MO subspace, in the AO-basis representation [33]. These matrices satisfy

𝐋2=𝐋,𝐑2=𝐑,(𝐈−𝐋)​𝐂~=0,𝐂~T​(𝐈−𝐑)=0.\mathbf{L}^{2}=\mathbf{L},\qquad\mathbf{R}^{2}=\mathbf{R},\qquad(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})\tilde{\mathbf{C}}=0,\qquad\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R})=0. (153)

The last two identities are the only ingredients needed to identify the forbidden component of a rank-nn variation. Applying the virtual projector on both AO indices of Eq. (150) gives

(𝐈−𝐋)​(δ​𝚲↑,↓)c​(𝐈−𝐑)\displaystyle(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})(\delta\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow})^{c}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R})
=(𝐈−𝐋)​δ​𝐂~​𝝀​𝐂~T​(𝐈−𝐑)⏟=0+(𝐈−𝐋)​𝐂~⏟=0​δ​𝝀​𝐂~T​(𝐈−𝐑)⏟=0+(𝐈−𝐋)​𝐂~⏟=0​𝝀​δ​𝐂~T​(𝐈−𝐑)\displaystyle=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})\delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}}\,\bm{\lambda}\,\underbrace{\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R})}_{=0}+\underbrace{(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})\tilde{\mathbf{C}}}_{=0}\,\delta\bm{\lambda}\,\underbrace{\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R})}_{=0}+\underbrace{(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})\tilde{\mathbf{C}}}_{=0}\,\bm{\lambda}\,\delta\tilde{\mathbf{C}}^{T}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R})
=0.\displaystyle=0. (154)

Thus, every first-order variation generated within the factorized rank-nn form has no virtual–virtual component:

(𝐈−𝐋)​(δ​𝚲↑,↓)c​(𝐈−𝐑)=0.(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})(\delta\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow})^{c}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R})=0. (155)

Equivalently, the virtual–virtual block is absent from the tangent space of the rank-nn AGP/SD ansatz. Therefore, the virtual–virtual component is the only component that must be removed from an arbitrary AO-basis variation in order to impose this linearized rank-nn constraint.

This observation gives a practical way to impose the rank constraint on an arbitrary optimization update. In other words, by eliminating the virtual–virtual component from a variation matrix, one can obtain a linearized rank-constrained update. The forbidden virtual–virtual component is

(δ​𝜶↑,↓)v​v=(𝐈−𝐋)​δ​𝜶↑,↓​(𝐈−𝐑).(\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow,\downarrow})_{vv}=(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow,\downarrow}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R}). (156)

Therefore, the constrained variation is obtained by subtracting only this forbidden component:

(δ​𝜶↑,↓)c=δ​𝜶↑,↓−(𝐈−𝐋)​δ​𝜶↑,↓​(𝐈−𝐑).(\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow,\downarrow})^{c}=\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow,\downarrow}-(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L})\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow,\downarrow}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R}). (157)

This projection leaves the occupied–occupied, occupied–virtual, and virtual–occupied components unchanged, while it removes the virtual–virtual component. Therefore, (δ​𝜶↑,↓)c(\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow,\downarrow})^{c} satisfies Eq. (155) and keeps the rank-nn AGP ansatz.

In this Subsection, δ​𝜶↑,↓\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow,\downarrow} denotes the matrix-valued variation of the paired geminal matrix 𝚲↑,↓\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow} in the AO basis, with matrix elements αl,l′↑,↓\alpha^{\uparrow,\downarrow}_{l,l^{\prime}} (dimension (Ma​o,Ma​o)(M_{ao},M_{ao})). In addition, the per-sample logarithmic derivative for paired-block parameters is treated as a matrix 𝐎paired\mathbf{O}^{\rm paired} with entries (𝐎paired)l,l′=∂log⁡Ψ/∂αl,l′↑,↓(\mathbf{O}^{\rm paired})_{l,l^{\prime}}=\partial\log\Psi/\partial\alpha^{\uparrow,\downarrow}_{l,l^{\prime}}. This differs from the 1D flattened index kk used in Secs. VI.1 and VI.2, where αk\alpha_{k} and OkO_{k} are scalars; the two views are related by unfolding the 1D index kk into the matrix index pair (l,l′)(l,l^{\prime}). The jQMC implementation matches this picture: the per-sample OO-matrix is held with a 1D parameter axis, and only the lambda block is temporarily reshaped to 2D for the projection.

In practice, the rank constraint of Eq. (157) is enforced not only directly on the final parameter update but also upstream on the per-sample logarithmic-derivative matrix 𝐎paired\mathbf{O}^{\rm paired}, from which the generalized force, the SR matrix, and the LM matrices are constructed [33, 8]. Specifically, the paired observable is replaced by

𝐎~paired=𝐎paired−(𝐈−𝐋T)​𝐎paired​(𝐈−𝐑T)\tilde{\mathbf{O}}^{\rm paired}\;=\;\mathbf{O}^{\rm paired}\;-\;(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{L}^{T})\,\mathbf{O}^{\rm paired}\,(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{R}^{T}) (158)

before any downstream optimization quantity is formed [33, 8]. After solving the SR/LM equations, the paired update is projected once more via Eq. (157) to exactly fulfill the rank constraint.

For spin-polarized systems with unpaired electrons, the geminal matrix in the AO-basis representation is composed of the spin-paired and spin-unpaired blocks (Eq. 51). Since the rank constraint originates from the paired block, F↑,↓F^{\uparrow,\downarrow}, the optimization constraint should be applied only to the paired geminal block 𝚲↑,↓\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow,\downarrow}. The unpaired block 𝚲↑\bm{\Lambda}^{\uparrow} carries no spin-down index and possesses no virtual–virtual subblock; neither the corresponding logarithmic derivative 𝐎unpaired\mathbf{O}^{\rm unpaired} nor the unpaired parameter update δ​𝜶↑\delta\bm{\alpha}^{\uparrow} is therefore subjected to any projection, and the unpaired part is optimized exactly as in the unconstrained SR/LM scheme of Secs. VI.1 and VI.2.

VII Implementation details

jQMC clearly separates data and algorithms. Data structures are implemented using Python dataclass. More specifically, we take the struct class from the flax library, which is compatible with JAX’s jit and grad. Algorithms are then defined as functions that take these data class instances, along with electron coordinates and control parameters. An overview of the data classes and algorithms used in jQMC is provided in Table 1, and the dependency relationships among the data classes are depicted as a diagram in Figure 1.

In jQMC, all computational kernels are JIT-compiled by JAX. These include the updates of electron positions in MCMC, the evaluation of eLe_{L} and ∂eL\partial e_{L}, and other observables, as well as the updates of electron positions in GFMC. In this sense, the numerically intensive kernels are executed on the GPU, while the CPU is used primarily for compilation and orchestration. The branching step in LRDMC, however, is still performed on CPUs. After the walker weights have been updated, the branching procedure based on these weights is executed on the CPU, because this step involves many conditional operations and also requires complex MPI communication associated with walker replication and deletion.

JAX transfers host data such as NumPy arrays from the CPU to the GPU when they are converted into JAX arrays or supplied to GPU-executed JAX computations. To avoid additional implementation complexity and to minimize repeated host–device transfers, we adopt a design in which the data required for the main numerical kernels is kept on the GPU whenever possible, while the memory demand on the GPU increases because most of the data required for the computation must reside in the GPU memory.

A typical workflow for performing LRDMC calculations with jQMC is illustrated in Figure 2. As it is standard in QMC simulations, the process begins by constructing a trial wave function, which typically requires input from HF or DFT calculations. jQMC supports the construction of trial wave functions via the TREX-IO interface, making it easy to import wave function data from many established ab initio electronic structure packages, such as PySCF [85]. Once the trial wave function is imported, one may proceed to optimize the Jastrow factor and, if necessary, the determinant part. After the wave function optimization is completed, one can perform single-point MCMC or LRDMC calculations. In the case of LRDMC, simulations are carried out with several lattice discretizations, and an extrapolation to the zero-lattice-spacing limit (a→0a\to 0) is performed to obtain unbiased energy estimates.

VIII Mixed-precision support

jQMC supports mixed-precision calculations. In jQMC, AO (except for gradients and Laplacian calculations) and Jastrow evaluations are performed using 32-bit floating-point (FP32). This works because the rounding errors in the AO evaluation from low-precision calculations are mitigated by the summation performed during MO calculations (in the case of SD) or geminal calculations (in the case of AGP), which are carried out in 64-bit floating-point (FP64). Furthermore, since the Jastrow term involves an exponential (exp\exp) function, its rounding errors from low-precision calculations are smoothed out by the exp\exp function. In particular, using FP32 in AO evaluations yields a significant speed-up because many computationally intensive exponential calculations are required for GTO evaluations, and single-precision transcendental operations such as exp\exp function are typically executed on special function units (SFUs), which are distinct from the main FP32/FP64 arithmetic pipelines [55]. Comparison of FP32/FP64 (mixed) and FP64 (full) calculations for water clusters is listed in Table 2. The table shows that both calculations yield energies that are consistent within the error bars (3​σ3\sigma) for all compounds (even when the number of electrons is increased up to 160), and that FP32/FP64 calculations are approximately twice as fast as the full-precision ones. We notice that users can switch between the full and mixed precisions via an input flag (the default is the full precision). In the following sections, full precision is used in Secs. X, XII, XIII, andXIV, whereas the mixed precision is used in Secs IX and XI.

IX Vectorization strategy

Within a single process, vectorization in jQMC is realized through JAX’s vmap function. In QMC algorithms, the top-level and most significant vectorization is over walkers. Since walkers in QMC simulations evolve nearly independently, batching over walkers provides the most natural and efficient way to exploit vectorization on modern hardware. As a result, to maximize single-GPU performance, especially in QMC algorithms where matrix-matrix or matrix-vector operations inside the inner loops are not dominant in computational cost, it is generally most efficient to assign as many walkers as possible to each GPU, up to the point where the GPU’s computational or memory throughput is saturated.

Figures 3 and 4 demonstrate the MCMC and LRDMC throughputs as the number of walkers per GPU is varied, for water clusters ranging from a single water molecule (Ne=8N_{e}=8) to a cluster of twenty water molecules (Ne=160N_{e}=160), using a single node of the Miyabi GPU cluster at the University of Tokyo. Notice that the throughput is the product of (i) the number of MCMC steps (or GFMC projections) executed per unit time by a single GPU multiplied by (ii) the number of walkers assigned to that GPU.

The benchmark calculations were performed using six water clusters: H2O (water, NeN_{e} = 8), (H2O)2 (water dimer NeN_{e} = 16), (H2O)4 (water cluster [4], NeN_{e} = 32), (H2O)6 (water cluster [6], NeN_{e} = 48), (H2O)10 (water cluster [8], NeN_{e} = 64), and (H2O)20 (water cluster [20], NeN_{e} = 160). We used the ccECP pseudopotentials accompanied with the cc-pVTZ basis set. As shown in Figs. 3 and 4, performance improves monotonically with the number of walkers per GPU, up to a saturation point. This saturation reflects the GPU becoming fully utilized, as analyzed in the next Section, and the corresponding walker count represents the most efficient configuration for that system. Since the optimal number of walkers per GPU depends on both the system size and hardware, users should perform preliminary benchmarking runs to identify the performance sweet spot before large-scale production simulations.

X Performance Analysis on NVIDIA GPU H100

In Section IX, we observed the throughputs of MCMC and LRDMC as the number of walkers increased, but it was unclear to what extent the GPU was actually utilized. Therefore, we used NVIDIA Nsight Systems and NVIDIA Nsight Compute to analyze how jQMC’s MCMC and LRDMC computations run on the GH200 chip of Miyabi Supercomputer. For the benchmark system, we used the water-cluster [8] (NeN_{e}=64) employed in Section IX.

Figure 5 shows a roofline plot for the function that calculates atomic orbitals with Cartesian GTOs for a given batched electron positions (dim. of input: (number of walkers, NeN_{e}, 3) →\rightarrow dim. of output: (number of walkers, number of AOs, NeN_{e})), which is the most basic computational function in jQMC. The x-axis plots the Arithmetic Intensity (AI), defined as floating-point operations (FLOPs) per byte, for the total data transfer involving (a) L1 cache, (b) L2 cache, and (c) DRAM (HBM3). In the roofline plot, each dot represents a (fused) CUDA kernel generated via XLA for different numbers of walkers, with wall time measured by NVIDIA Nsight Compute used to size the circles. The plot reveals that a single fused CUDA kernel dominates most of the AO computation. We focus on the kernel hereafter. Up to Nw=2048N_{w}=2048, the achieved number of floating-point operations per second (FLOPS or FLOP/s) increases as the number of walkers, resulting in the achieved FLOPS of 5.65 and the AI of 817.32. The achieved FLOPS is about 22% of the peak FLOPS of the CUDA 64-bit kernel. However, the achieved FLOPS are saturated after Nw=2048N_{w}=2048, and the kernel point just shifts to the left (i.e., the AI decreases) without increasing FLOPS. Finally, none of the CUDA kernels are on the L1, L2, DRAM rooflines, even with Nw=32768N_{w}=32768. NVIDIA Nsight Compute reveals that the bottleneck is neither L1, L2, nor DRAM BW (i.e., the bytes/s sustained between the Streaming Multiprocessors and each memory tier, as drawn by the roofline ceilings), but the L1 wavefront pipe (i.e., the transactions/cycle throughput of the L1 load/store unit, which is distinct from its byte BW when warp threads access non-contiguous addresses [56]). Figure 6 plots, as a function of NwN_{w}, the achieved fraction of the peak of five quantities. The dashed lines (L1 byte BW, L2 byte BW) and the DRAM byte BW curve report the bytes/s delivered by the kernel normalized by the device-peak BW of each level, which correspond to the ceilings of the hierarchical roofline of Fig. 5. The two solid lines, in contrast, report a transaction-rate occupancy: L1 LSU (Load Store Unit) wavefront pipe is the number of wavefronts/cycle issued through the L1 load/store data pipe normalized by its peak, and L2 request pipe is the analogous quantity at the L2 boundary. Figure 6 reveals that the L1 LSU wavefront pipe reaches ∼90%\sim 90\% of peak for Nw=2048N_{w}=2048, while L1 byte BW shows plateaus near ∼50%\sim 50\%. We notice that the ∼40\sim 40-point gap between the solid and the dashed red curves is invisible on the byte-only roofline yet identifies the kernel as L1 transaction-throughput bound rather than L1 BW bound. The L2 request pipe stays at a lower absolute level (peaking near ∼48%\sim 48\%), indicating that the L1 absorbing is most of the gather traffic. DRAM byte BW only becomes appreciable at the largest Nw=32768N_{w}=32768, where the working set finally exceeds the on-chip L1 and L2 caches. These results suggest that cache optimizations will be necessary for future improvements in FLOPS and AI performance. In addition, we analyzed each component, such as continuum kinetic energy, discretized kinetic energy, and non-local ECP computations, which are dominant in the computation of the local energy in MCMC and the projection in LRDMC. For example, Figure 7 shows the roofline plot for the discretized kinetic energy computation (Eq. 21) with Nw=2048N_{w}=2048. The plot shows that the dominant (fused) CUDA kernels are all in DRAM-bound regions, suggesting that QMC calculations as a whole are also dominated by memory-bound operations. The bottleneck of each kernel depends on whether it is L1-, L2-, or DRAM-limited, according to our Compute analysis with NVIDIA Nsight Compute, and the optimization must be tailored to the specific circumstances. The CUDA-kernel-level optimization (i.e., via high-level operations (HLO) generated by JAX) for jQMC is an interesting future work.

XI Wall-time benchmark

The walltime required in practice for MCMC and LRDMC calculations depends strongly on the quality of the employed wave function, because the ultimate target of QMC simulations is the statistical error bar, and the efficiency for reaching a given error bar is significantly affected by the wave-function quality. Since different QMC packages adopt different wave-function parameterizations and different functional forms of the Jastrow factor, a fair comparison between packages is generally difficult. However, TurboRVB and jQMC use the same Jastrow factor, enabling a genuinely fair comparison. In this benchmark, we prepared exactly the same Jastrow–Slater ansatz in both TurboRVB and jQMC, and compared the absolute wall-clock time required to achieve a target statistical accuracy of 1 kcal/mol in the total energy for a given ansatz. Parameters related to computational efficiency, such as the electron hopping distance used in the MCMC proposal, the frequency of observable calculations in MCMC, and the lattice discretization mesh and projection time in LRDMC, were set to the same values for both TurboRVB and jQMC.

Benchmark calculations were carried out for six systems of increasing size: water (Ne=8N_{e}=8), water dimer (Ne=16N_{e}=16), water cluster [4] (Ne=32N_{e}=32), water cluster [6] (Ne=48N_{e}=48), water cluster [8] (Ne=64N_{e}=64), and water cluster [20] (Ne=160N_{e}=160). All calculations employed the ccECP pseudopotentials together with the cc-pVTZ basis set. For the determinant part, we directly used the orbitals obtained from an LDA-PZ DFT calculation with PySCF-forge. TurboRVB employs spherical GTOs, whereas jQMC supports both spherical and Cartesian GTOs. Since the Cartesian representation is faster than the Spherical one in jQMC, we transformed the orbitals from spherical to Cartesian form for the jQMC calculations; the physical energy is, of course, unchanged by this transformation. For the Jastrow factor, we used J=J2+J3J=J_{2}+J_{3}, where J2J_{2} was of Padé type and J3J_{3} was expanded in localized atomic orbitals, using H:[3s1p] and O:[4s2p1d]. The variational parameters of the Jastrow factor were optimized in TurboRVB, and the resulting values were copied into the Jastrow_data of jQMC. Using these wave functions, we computed the total energy and variance with both TurboRVB and jQMC by MCMC, and confirmed that the results agreed within the statistical error bars for all six systems.

For these wave functions, we prepared one node (equipped with two multi-core CPUs with four GPUs) on the Genkai supercomputer, and measured the time required to achieve a statistical error bar of 1 kcal/mol in two cases: using CPUs only and using CPU+GPUs (TurboRVB) or only GPUs (jQMC). In the CPU-only calculations, both TurboRVB and jQMC used 120 MPI processes, corresponding to the maximum number available of cores on a single node, with one walker assigned to each MPI process. In the GPU calculations with jQMC, one MPI process was bound to each GPU, and the number of walkers per MPI process was chosen to maximize the MCMC and LRDMC throughput on the Genkai GPU node. In contrast, TurboRVB does not implement walker-level vectorization, unlike jQMC; instead, NVIDIA CUDA MPS was used [9], and 30 MPI processes (i.e., all cores in one NUMA domain, which is the optimal setting for the CPU-bound part, despite possibly oversubscribing a single GPU) were assigned to each GPU. The compilation and runtime environments are summarized in Table 4.

Figure 8 shows the absolute node-seconds required to reach a statistical error bar of 1 kcal/mol in the total energy for the systems listed above. Focusing first on jQMC, one can clearly see that GPU acceleration yields speedups exceeding two orders of magnitude, if compared with the same calculations run on CPUs. This is consistent with expectations, since JAX has been developed with GPU execution in mind. By contrast, in TurboRVB, the GPU calculations are slower than the CPU calculations for the system sizes and hardware configurations tested here. This is because TurboRVB does not parallelize at the walker level, as noted above, and only partially offloads the computation to the GPU by replacing some matrix and vector operations (BLAS/LAPACK) with cuBLAS and cuSolver routines. In TurboRVB, the GPU version becomes more advantageous as the system size increases because kernels replaced with cuBLAS and cuSolver are more dominant; Fig. 8 demonstrates that for systems with roughly Ne∼100N_{e}\sim 100, GPU acceleration becomes clearly beneficial, particularly in the LRDMC implementation. We expect that for even larger systems, the GPU version of TurboRVB will eventually be faster than the CPU one.

Figure 8 also shows that the current CPU version of jQMC is about 10 times slower than TurboRVB on the same CPU (Intel Xeon Platinum 8490H), even though jQMC implements essentially the same algorithm to the best of our knowledge. This indicates that the current jQMC is suboptimal on CPU via XLA. For instance, using hardware-counter measurements, we found that JAX/XLA emits mostly scalar instructions in the AO kernel, with only a small amount of AVX2 and almost no AVX-512, even though the CPU supports them; forcing a 512-bit preferred vector width does not change this, pointing to a code-structure rather than a flag issue. After rewriting the relevant part of the AO kernel, we obtained a speedup of a factor of 2 for the AO evaluation (c.f., We did not merge this change because it made the GPU version slightly slower). In contrast, a minimal Fortran/C implementation of the same operation, compiled with the Intel compiler, is almost fully vectorized with AVX-512 and is much faster (about 6 times over the baseline) than the JAX AO kernel. Beyond the AO kernel, there are most likely further CPU-side bottlenecks in other kernels of jQMC, which we leave for future identification. The current jQMC layout is well suited to GPU but remains suboptimal for CPU; a unified implementation that performs well on both is left for future work.

Comparing the two faster cases in each package, jQMC on GPUs with TurboRVB on CPUs, jQMC is faster for both MCMC and LRDMC in the wall times, thanks to GPUs. The jQMC MCMC and LRDMC are faster than the corresponding TurboRVB calculations by 10 times and 3 times, respectively, for the system sizes taken into account here. In the LRDMC calculations, the speed-up offered by jQMC is not as drastic as that found in MCMC. This is because, in LRDMC, the computational bottleneck involves a significant amount of AO evaluations, needed in the discretized kinetic energy and in the non-local ECP calculations, resulting in a performance gain that are not as significant as those achieved with MCMC. Further acceleration is expected if AO calculations can be made more optimal in jQMC. Nevertheless, the present benchmark demonstrates that jQMC has already been tuned to deliver wall-clock performance comparable to, or even better than, TurboRVB, despite the fact that TurboRVB is a long-optimized Fortran90 code benefiting from Intel Fortran compiler optimizations.

XII Parallelization strategy: Weak scaling benchmarks

Although the vectorization scheme described above improves the throughput on a single GPU, production QMC calculations often require simulations that exceed the capacity of a single device. In jQMC, multi-GPU calculations are therefore supported by explicit MPI-based parallelization via mpi4py for CPUs or by the sharding mechanisms provided by JAX for GPUs. We examined the weak-scaling performance of jQMC on the Miyabi and Leonardo supercomputers. The benchmark target is the water cluster (H2O)20 (Ne=160N_{e}=160). In these benchmarks, the number of walkers per GPU is fixed at 100, while the number of GPUs was increased, allowing us to assess the implementation’s parallel efficiency in realistic multi-GPU settings.

Figure 9 shows the weak-scaling benchmark results for (a) VMC (MCMC sampling + one step of wave function optimization ) and (b) LRDMC. As seen, the weak-scaling behavior differs between VMC and LRDMC. In the VMC case [Fig. 9(a)], the performance initially improves as the number of walkers increases, both on Miyabi and Leonardo. This improvement is attributed to the faster convergence of the CG solver when the number of walkers per GPU, and hence the total number of MCMC samples, is increased. With an even larger number of walkers, a slight degradation is observed on Miyabi, whereas the good weak-scaling performance is maintained up to 1024 GPUs on Leonardo. The slowdown on Miyabi is likely due to network latency and/or hardware-induced GPU-to-GPU performance variability across different GPUs, which has not yet been identified. Nevertheless, the weak-scaling efficiency remains close to unity on Miyabi (1.02), while Leonardo maintains good performance (0.92) up to 1024 GPUs, corresponding to 102,400 walkers. In the LRDMC case [Fig. 9(b)], the slowdown is observed as the number of walkers increases on both Miyabi and Leonardo. This behavior is expected since LRDMC requires inter-walker communication between two consecutive branching steps, as described in Sec. II.2.2. Here, we compare two branching schemes for LRDMC: the conventional algorithm [13] and the load-balanced algorithm [51]. As expected, the load-balanced algorithm shows better weak-scaling performance than the conventional one on both Miyabi and Leonardo, because it is specifically designed to balance the computational workload among walkers [51]. Both LRDMC algorithms maintain performance close to unity up to 512 GPUs on Miyabi and 256 GPUs on Leonardo. A more pronounced degradation is observed at 1024 GPUs on Miyabi and 512 GPUs on Leonardo, likely again due to network latency and/or hardware-induced GPU-to-GPU performance variability. Nevertheless, the load-balanced LRDMC algorithm still achieves good weak-scaling performance, with values of ∼\sim 1.2 on Miyabi and ∼\sim 1.1 on Leonardo, for the largest calculations considered, corresponding to 102,400 walkers. These benchmarks demonstrate that the MPI- and GPU-parallel implementation introduces only a small overhead over the present range of system sizes, both for VMC and LRDMC.

XIII Verification of the code

XIII.1 Intra-software tests

The intra-software tests in jQMC are designed according to the following principle. Achieving high computational performance with JAX requires jit compilation and vmap vectorization. They may obscure the underlying algorithmic flow and make it more difficult to debug the code than conventional Python implementations. To address the trade-off between performance and maintainability, jQMC adopts a dual-implementation strategy. More specifically, for the main functions, two versions are implemented in parallel: a production version without a suffix and a corresponding debug version with the suffix _debug. The production version is used for production calculations and is highly optimized for performance. By contrast, the _debug version prioritizes readability by using standard Python constructs, allowing users and developers to follow the logic step by step. Then, to ensure correctness, we implement consistency tests for as many function pairs as possible. These tests verify that the production and debug implementations produce equivalent results. The CD/CI framework on GitHub triggers pytest every time a change is pushed or nightly. Every Python module is accompanied by a corresponding test Python module. For example, test_wavefunction.py contains comprehensive tests for the dataclasses and associated functions defined in wavefunction.py. These tests help reduce the risk of introducing bugs, thereby improving the maintainability and reliability of jQMC.

XIII.2 Inter-software tests

In the QMC community, recent efforts have been made to systematically examine reproducibility across multiple codes [21]. One notable study involved 11 different community-developed QMC codes and focused on computing the total energy and binding energy of the water–methane dimer. These calculations were performed using a common basis set (cc-pVTZ) and a common pseudopotential (ccECP), allowing a controlled investigation of reproducibility across implementations. In DMC calculations employing ECPs, one of the technical challenges is how to deal with the non-local part of the ECP. Approaches such as the Locality Approximation (LA) and T-move (TM) are known to affect the zero-time-step (t→0t\rightarrow 0) limit. This is due not only to the non-local part treatment, but also to the amplitude of the wave function, set by the Jastrow factor. As a result, differences in Jastrow implementations among codes can lead to discrepancies in energies. On the other hand, the Determinant Locality Approximation (DLA) and DLA combined with TM (DTM) yield significantly better agreement among codes, as it minimizes sensitivity to the specific form of the Jastrow factor in the small-tt or small-aa limits. We carry out calculations analogous to the consistency test in the aforementioned reproducibility study corresponding to the DTM locality approximation (i.e., we used LRDMC with DLA) to assess the consistency of our implementation. We present our validation results in Fig. 10 and Table. 5.

XIV Demonstrations: VMC and LRDMC atomic forces with optimized JSD ansatz

Recently, the quantitative disagreement between CCSD(T) [64] and FN-DMC with a Jastrow–Slater determinant ansatz has been actively discussed. In particular, since the report of discrepancies of up to about 8 kcal/mol for the binding energies of dispersion-dominated systems, such as C60 encapsulated in a [6]cycloparaphenyleneacetylene ring (C60+5PPA), reported by Al-Hamdani and co-workers [3], the origin of these discrepancies has been debated from both the CCSD(T) and DMC perspectives [24, 72, 50]. Beyond total energies, first derivatives, namely atomic forces, have also been examined. For the same molecular structures, Slootman et al. computed the differences between CCSD(T) and FN-DMC forces for ethanol [76]. They reported that, for ethanol, DMC forces agree with all-electron CCSD(T) within a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.5 kcal mol-1 Å-1, even when the Reynolds approximation is employed (Eq. 103). In the present work, we extend this comparison by performing LRDMC force calculations for ethanol and malonaldehyde, both included in the rMD17 set [19, 20], and assessing their agreement with CCSD(T).

As in Ref. 46, we selected ethanol and malonaldehyde from the rMD17 dataset [19, 20], and computed (i) VMC forces with fully optimized wave functions, (ii) LRDMC forces using trial wave functions fully optimized at the VMC level, (iii) Hartree–Fock (HF), second-order Møller–Plesset perturbation theory (MP2), CCSD, and DFT forces, and (iv) CCSD(T) forces as references. We extracted 50 structures for each molecule from the rMD17 dataset [19, 20]. We employed the cc-pVQZ basis set for the HF, MP2 [43], and CCSD [63], and CCSD(T) calculations. We employed def2-QZVPPD [94] basis set for DFT calculations with the SVWN [92], PBE [59], B3LYP [83], PBE0+D3BJ [2], or ω\omegaB97M+D3BJ [34, 44] functionals. In the MP2, CCSD, and CCSD(T) calculations, the 1ss core orbitals were kept frozen. The HF, DFT, MP2, CCSD, and CCSD(T) calculations were performed using the Psi4 software suite (version 1.9.1) [77]. For the VMC and LRDMC calculations, we used ccECP [10] together with the corresponding cc-pVTZ basis sets. The MO coefficients in the Slater determinant and the parameters in the Jastrow factor were optimized variationally at the VMC level. The Jastrow factor included inhomogeneous one-body (Eq. 29), two-body (Eq. 32), and three-body (Eq. 35) terms. For the basis sets of the inhomogeneous one-body and three-body Jastrow terms, we used uncontracted primitive GTOs with [3s1p] for H and [4s2p1d] for C, N, and O. The Gaussian exponents were optimized for each configuration during the wave-function optimization. The total numbers of optimized variational parameters were 38233 and 54749 for ethanol and malonaldehyde, respectively. The trial wave functions were generated with PySCF-forge [85].

To compare the methods considered here, we computed the pairwise MAEs between their force predictions and displayed them as a heat map in Fig. 11. The computed VMC and LRDMC forces carry statistical errors. Suppose that the error bar of each force component is an independent Gaussian random variable, εi,I∼𝒩⁡(0,σi,I2)\varepsilon_{i,I}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{i,I}^{2}), where ii and II denote sample index and force component. Since the MAE is computed using |di,I|≡|Δ​Fi,I+εi,I||d_{i,I}|\equiv|\Delta F_{i,I}+\varepsilon_{i,I}|, the measured MAE is always biased by the statistical errors. Indeed, even when the two methods agree exactly (Δ​Fi,I=0\Delta F_{i,I}=0), the obtained MAE does not vanish but reaches a floor,

MAEfloor=𝔼⁡[|εi,I|]=2π​⟨σi,I⟩,\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{floor}}=\mathbb{E}[|\varepsilon_{i,I}|]=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\,\langle\sigma_{i,I}\rangle, (159)

where the brackets denote the average over all samples and force components. Notice that σi,I=[(σi,IA)2+(σi,IB)2]1/2\sigma_{i,I}=[(\sigma^{A}_{i,I})^{2}+(\sigma^{B}_{i,I})^{2}]^{1/2} when both methods are stochastic and independent. In the present calculations, the MAE floors are 0.35 and 0.72 kcal mol-1 Å-1 for VMC and LRDMC in ethanol, respectively (0.82 kcal mol-1 Å-1 when VMC is compared with LRDMC), and 0.33 and 1.13 kcal mol-1 Å-1 in malonaldehyde, repectively (1.20 kcal mol-1 Å-1 for VMC vs LRDMC). Unless the measured MAE clearly exceeds this floor, we cannot conclude that there is a genuine difference between the two methods.

For ethanol, Slootman et al. [76] reported a benchmark result for 200 configurations. Their calculation yielded an MAE of 3.055 kcal mol-1 Å-1 for VMC forces, with respect to the CCSD(T) values taken as reference. Our MAE on VMC forces for ethanol, (2.5 kcal mol-1) in MAE, is lower than theirs, likely because of the more flexible Jastrow factor used in the present study. We note, however, that our ethanol configurations are not identical to theirs and MAEs have the uncertainty as noted above, so this is not a strict one-to-one comparison. Slootman et al. also reported an MAE of 2.0 kcal mol-1 Å-1 for DMC forces evaluated with the Reynolds approximation. In our calculations, we obtained a similar MAE of 2.1 kcal mol-1 Å-1 for ethanol, which is close to the value reported by Slootman et al.

For malonaldehyde, one of the authors of the present study previously reported a large discrepancy between VMC and CCSD(T) forces in Ref. 46, amounting to 7.2 kcal mol-1 Å-1 in RMSE (4.8 kcal mol-1 Å-1 in MAE). We reproduce the same inconsistency in the present study, obtaining an MAE of 5.8 kcal mol-1 Å-1 for the MCMC forces. The obtained MAE differs from the value reported in Ref. 46 by 1 kcal mol-1 Å-1. We attribute the difference mainly to variations in the trial wave functions employed in the two calculations. In this study, jQMC uses the exponential form for the two-body Jastrow factor, whereas the previous work uses the Padé form. In addition, the trial wave functions were generated using different XC functionals, namely B3LYP and LDA-PZ in the present and previous works, respectively. Finally, the GTOs used in the three-body Jastrow factor also differ between the two calculations, namely, Cartesian and Spherical GTOs, respectively (i.e., the number of dd orbitals are different).

Interestingly, even LRDMC shows a large discrepancy relative to CCSD(T), with an MAE of 5.2 kcal mol-1 Å-1. Since the trial wave function, including its nodal surface, was optimized at the VMC level, the mean-field nodal surface is unlikely to be the primary origin of the discrepancy. The reason for the significant deviation in malonaldehyde is not yet fully understood and will require further investigation from both the DMC and CCSD(T) perspectives.

XV Conclusions and perspectives

In this work, we presented the implementation details and benchmark results of jQMC, a Python-based ab initio quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) package built on top of JAX. jQMC is designed with modern heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) architectures in mind, particularly those combining CPUs and GPUs, which are rapidly becoming mainstream. The code is parallelized at the top level of QMC algorithms, i.e., based on a multi-walker strategy. By packing as many walkers as GPU memory permits, jQMC fully leverages GPU computational power, leading to significant acceleration of QMC simulations. Benchmark results confirm the effectiveness of this design.

jQMC remains under active development, and several important directions can be envisaged. From a physics perspective, the implementation of periodic boundary conditions is a major milestone for future work, which is in progress and will be most likely supported in the next release. From a performance point of view, improving cache and memory efficiencies is an urgent challenge. While future hardware advancements may alleviate this issue, software-level solutions will also be essential.

XVI Code and Data availability

The code and data that support the findings of this study are available from GitHub repositories [https://github.com/jqmc-project/jQMC] and [https://github.com/jqmc-project/jQMC-data], respectively. All calculations in this work were performed using jQMC version corresponding to v0.2.2.
